items.title: RDC: Aubin Minaku, ancien président de l'Assemblée nationale placé en résidence surveillée
items.description: En République démocratique du Congo, l’ancien président de l’Assemblée nationale Aubin Minaku n’est plus détenu dans un cachot secret. Après dix mois de détention sous la responsabilité du Conseil national de cyberdéfense, qui dépend de la présidence, puis de la justice militaire, Minaku a été transféré mardi soir à son domicile, dans la capitale. Il y est désormais placé en résidence surveillée, sous la garde de militaires. Une mesure qui intervient alors que le PPRD, dont il est le vice-président national, a été dissous par la justice, sur fond de rapprochement entre son autorité morale et la rébellion dans l’Est du pays.

items.title: We’ll defeat Nigeria’s enemies, Tinubu declares in Jigawa
items.description: •Vice-President claims all four former governors back APC •Says North should reciprocate Tinubu’s support; tackles Amaechi over Buhari remarks •President has won enemies of democracy – Yari By Omeiza Ajayi & Muhammad Inuwa ABUJA – President Bola Tinubu has vowed to defeat those he described as enemies of Nigeria’s unity and stability, telling supporters at his ruling All Progressives Congress APC presidential campaign rally in Dutse, the Jigawa State capital, that the fight against insecurity will be won. Read Also: 2027: Security tops as APC-PCC unveils 4-point manifesto Speaking on Tuesday, the President acknowledged the security worries of his audience. “I know you have problems of insecurity in Nigeria, but working together, see your neighbour as your friend and partner. See the individual, exchange information, anything you know about insecurity, report it immediately. We have been through many wars. We will defeat our enemies. Enemies of unity, enemies of stability, enemies of all. “We have strengthened the police, we have strengthened the armed forces, we are paying better salaries today,” he said, promising that the forces would be well taken care of in housing and rewards, “regardless of where they come from.” He also dismissed talk that fuel subsidy would return. “To those who say subsidy is coming back, it’s a lie. Don’t let them lie to you again,” he said. On agriculture, Tinubu promised relief for farmers and lower food prices. “Interest-free loan for farmers is coming. Prosperity is coming. Food security will happen. We are going to instal mechanised farming service centre in six geographical locations”, the president said. He said universities would do more research and development in agriculture than ever before. “We have the arable land, we have the commitment, we have the people. We can feed ourselves and we will bring the food prices down to the minimum,” he said. The President pointed to road projects as proof that no region had been left behind, and defended his education financing. He described the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) as “a weapon against poverty,” and said money recovered by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission EFCC would go to it. “Every money recovered from irregularities by EFCC is now directed to NELFUND to educate our children. Every asset through irregularities will be invested in NELFUND,” he said. Tinubu said he had commissioned a skill development centre on his way from the airport, and congratulated Governor Umar Namadi. He then presented the APC manifesto, listing its commitments to lives saved, a lower cost of living, reliable power, a stronger industrial base, support for small and medium businesses and wider job opportunities. He also listed quality health care, 20,000 additional teachers, health insurance expanded for more than 23 million people, affordable homes and secure lands, and a responsible and accountable government. “With a very strong commitment, today we present to you our roadmap to prosperity, the manifesto of our party. I once again launch the manifesto of our party to the glory of God almighty and prosperity of Nigeria”, he added. Earlier, Director General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Senator Abdul’aziz Yari recalled how opponents were campaigning that Tinubu would not be welcomed in northern Nigeria. “Your Excellency, Mr President, these are your people, men and women and youths. This is Northwest, where our opponents are campaigning that you are not going to be welcomed in the northern Nigeria,” Yari said. He praised Tinubu’s record on democracy. “You show you are a real democrat, you have suffered for this democracy to be sustained, you have interfaced with the enemies of democracy and you won them. Today, they are enjoying your sweat,” he said. Yari said Tinubu’s opponents had nothing more to offer than what the President had done for Nigeria and for the North. He challenged those who call themselves “core northerners” to show that they had supported a councillor, a local government chairman or a governor to victory, as Tinubu had. He recounted a request he made of the President in Saudi Arabia, asking him to pray for the success of the team. “He said, Abduraziz, you are already successful because Allah is with us and we are here to pray,” Yari said. Jigawa belongs to APC, even Lamido is with us — Shettima Vice President Kashim Shettima has declared Jigawa State an All Progressives Congress, APC stronghold, claiming that all four former governors of the state, including former Governor Sule Lamido, are supporting the ruling party ahead of the 2027 general elections. Shettima made the claim on Tuesday at the APC presidential campaign rally in Dutse, the state capital, where he expressed confidence that President Bola Tinubu would secure massive votes in Jigawa. He named former governors Ali Sa’adu, Ibrahim Saminu Turaki, Muhammad Badaru Abubakar and Sule Lamido as political figures backing the APC. “Jigawa State is a home for the APC. All who and who, any politician who answers a name is with us. The former governors of Jigawa State, Ali Sa’adu, Ibrahim Saminu Turaki, Muhammad Badaru Abubakar, and even former Governor Alhaji Sule Lamido, are with us,” he said. The Vice-President urged Jigawa residents to vote for Tinubu and other APC candidates, arguing that the North should reciprocate the President’s support for the region and its people. He called on voters to turn out in large numbers, expressing confidence that the ruling party would record a landslide victory in the state. Shettima also criticised the African Democratic Congress, ADC, vice-presidential candidate, Rotimi Amaechi, over his reported comments accusing the late former President Muhammadu Buhari of deceiving him. Describing the remarks as disrespectful to the North, Shettima said Buhari remained one of the most respected political figures in the region. He said Northerners were known for their generosity and tradition of appreciating and reciprocating good gestures. The Vice-President urged the electorate to support Tinubu, insisting that the 2027 election offered an opportunity for the North to demonstrate its appreciation of the President’s actions towards the region. items.title: Where will the money come from? MP questions 24-hour economy funding
items.description: The proposed financing model for the government’s 24-hour economy programme could come under pressure in 2027 if revenue targets are not met, the MP for Manso Nkwanta, Tweneboa Kodua Fokuo, has warned. He said the government’s plan to create fiscal space for the programme depended heavily on revenue expected to be generated in the future, rather than funds already available. That, he said, raised questions about the sustainability of the initiative, particularly with the economy projected to grow at a slower rate in 2027. Speaking on the PM Express on Joy News on Tuesday, November 10, ahead of the presentation of the 2027 Budget by the Finance Minister, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, Mr Fokuo said the government could struggle to finance the programme if revenue mobilisation fell short of expectations. “It’s not as if we have the money at hand now. No, we don’t have the money now,” he said. He explained that the financing arrangement appeared to rely on a proposed adjustment to the primary surplus target from 1.5 per cent to 0.5 per cent, creating room in the budget for spending on the programme. However, he cautioned that the anticipated fiscal space was dependent on revenue that the government was yet to collect. Mr Fokuo said the projected slowdown in economic growth from 6.2 per cent in 2026 to 4.9 per cent in 2027 could further complicate revenue mobilisation and place the programme’s funding under strain. “If you look at revenue that has been generated this year, even when the economy is growing at 6.2 per cent, versus 2027 that we are projecting to slow down to 4.9, what it means is that we are likely to struggle in terms of revenue for 2027,” he said. He consequently questioned where the resources to support the programme would come from if government revenue underperformed. “If we do struggle for 2027, then you ask yourself where would the funding for the new economy really come from?” he asked. Financing concerns Mr Fokuo also questioned the earlier approach to financing the 24-hour economy, saying the private sector had failed to respond as expected because the programme was announced without adequate measures to manage the risks associated with participation. He said the absence of a clear risk-management framework had weakened private-sector appetite for the initiative, leaving government to consider a financing arrangement that placed greater responsibility on the public purse. “When the private sector did not jump on board as was expected, because it was just a slogan, it was just a pronouncement, but nothing was done to really manage the risks thereof, the private sector had no interest,” he said. He described the current arrangement as a repackaging of the programme, with government funding expected to play a more prominent role. The MP’s comments come as attention turns to the 2027 Budget, which is expected to provide further details on the government’s economic priorities, revenue projections and financing plans. The budget will be closely watched for clarity on how the government intends to fund the 24-hour economy initiative, attract private investment and ensure that its commitments are supported by sustainable revenue sources.

items.title: Leave politics to politicians, northern minorities tell clerics
items.description: By Henry Umoru ABUJA — Ahead of the 2027 general elections, the Northern Nigeria Minorities Group, NNMG, has cautioned religious leaders, particularly imams and pastors, against partisan political involvement and the use of churches and mosques as platforms for political mobilisation. The group, which represents more than 200 minority communities across Northern Nigeria and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), urged religious leaders to distinguish their spiritual responsibilities from partisan political activities, warning that inflammatory political messages from religious platforms could heighten tensions and expose Nigerians to violence. Addressing journalists in Abuja yesterday, the Convener, Jacob Edi, also known as Kakaki Bassange, said religious leaders should focus on praying for the peace and unity of the country, while leaving partisan politics to politicians. He said: “Politics is for politicians, religion is for pastors and imams. They should pray for this nation. They should pray for the peace and unity of Nigeria. “When a pastor or an imam tells you about peace, he is not looking for your vote. He is not even looking for your money. This is his duty. This is his calling.” Edi said anyone interested in partisan politics should relinquish religious leadership and join a political party to pursue such ambitions. “If he wants to come into politics, he should remove the garment or remove the jalabia or whatever and go to any party,” he said. The group also cautioned opposition politicians against actions capable of destabilising the country, urging them to resolve political disagreements through constitutional and judicial processes. Vanguard News The post Leave politics to politicians, northern minorities tell clerics appeared first on Vanguard News .

Nigeria’s private sector foreign debt rise 179.6% to $54.5bn — World Bank
items.description: By Babajide Komolafe The World Bank said that the foreign debt of Nigerian companies rose by 179.6 per cent in seven years to $54.48 billion in 2025 from $19.49 billion in 2018. This implies that Nigerian businesses now owe foreign lenders almost three times what they owed in 2018. The World Bank disclosed this in its International Debt Report 2026 which stated that Nigeria’s private sector nonguaranteed external debt stood at $54.476 billion as of December 2025. The World Bank explained that the total external debt of a country is the sum of public and publicly guaranteed debt, private nonguaranteed debt, and short-term debt. According to the World Bank, private sector nonguaranteed external debt refers to money borrowed by private companies from foreign banks, investors and other lenders without the government or any public institution guaranteeing repayment. “Private nonguaranteed debt comprises long-term external obligations of private debtors that are not guaranteed by a public entity. “Public and publicly guaranteed external debt comprises long-term external obligations (maturities of over one year) of all public debtors, including debt held by the central government and by state-owned enterprises. Short-term debt is defined as debt with an original maturity of one year or less ,” the report said. The 179.6 per cent growth in Nigeria’s private sector in the seven years was faster than the increase in government-backed external debt, which rose by 155.5 per cent from $24.422 billion in 2018 to $62.4 billion in 2025. The World Bank report showed that private companies’ foreign debt is becoming an increasingly important part of Nigeria’s external debt burden. In 2018, private sector nonguaranteed debt was equivalent to about 79.8 per cent of public and publicly guaranteed external debt. By 2025, it had increased to 87.3 per cent. Meanwhile, Nigeria’s total external debt, covering government borrowing, private companies’ foreign loans and short-term obligations, increased from $46.238 billion in 2018 to $145.015 billion in 2025. The report also highlighted the high cost of borrowing from private foreign lenders. According to the World Bank, new loans obtained by Nigeria from private foreign creditors in 2025 attracted an average interest rate of 9.6 per cent, compared with 1.9 per cent for loans from official creditors such as governments and multilateral institutions. Private lenders also offered an average repayment period of 12 years, compared with 25 years for official creditors. The post Nigeria’s private sector foreign debt rise 179.6% to $54.5bn — World Bank appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: ‘New economy is repackaged 24-hour economy’ – Manso Nkwanta MP
items.description: The proposed “new economy” being advanced by the government is largely a rebranding of the 24-hour economy policy, with the key difference being a shift towards public financing after efforts to attract private sector investment failed, the MP for Manso Nkwanta, Tweneboa Kodua Fokuo, has said. He argued that the economic pillars underpinning the two initiatives were essentially the same, particularly their emphasis on export expansion, import substitution and accelerated national development. Mr Fokuo, who is the Deputy Ranking Member of Parliament’s Economy and Development Committee, said the government appeared to be presenting the 24-hour economy agenda in a different form, with public funds now expected to play a more prominent role in its implementation. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, November 10, ahead of the presentation of the 2027 Budget by the Finance Minister, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, he questioned whether the proposed new economic direction represented a fundamental departure from the earlier policy. “If you look at what is being described as a new economy, in reality, it is not different from the 24-hour economy,” he said. He explained that the 24-hour economy, particularly its expanded “24-hour economy plus” component, had also been designed to accelerate development through increased exports and the replacement of imported goods with locally produced alternatives. According to him, the pillars now being associated with the new economy closely mirror those previously outlined under the 24-hour economy programme. The MP said a major challenge with the earlier initiative was its reliance on private sector financing, which, in his assessment, failed to attract the level of interest required to make the programme successful. “It does seem that the 24-hour economy was positioned as a programme that would be financed by the private sector, and that could not materialise. The private sector had no appetite at all for the 24-hour economy programme,” he said. Mr Fokuo argued that the government’s current approach appeared to be a re-presentation of the same policy, but with public financing taking centre stage. He said the forthcoming 2027 Budget would provide an opportunity to examine the government’s proposed economic direction, including how it intended to finance its programmes and translate its policy ambitions into measurable outcomes. The Finance Minister is expected to present the 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy to Parliament, setting out the government’s spending priorities, revenue measures and economic plans for the coming year.

items.title: Demystifying Derivatives: Yield enhancement through equity and credit-linked solutions (Part 1)
items.description: Institutional investors traditionally gain exposure to equities and bonds by purchasing the underlying securities directly. While this approach remains central to portfolio construction, direct investment can sometimes present practical constraints, particularly when investors seek exposure to assets listed or issued outside their domestic markets. Derivatives can provide an alternative route. When combined with traditional deposits, they can create structured solutions whose returns are linked to the performance of equities, market indices, corporate debt or sovereign credit. These structures allow investors to gain exposure to selected markets without necessarily purchasing or holding the underlying securities directly. Equity-Linked Deposits and Credit-Linked Deposits illustrate how this can be achieved. Both can expand the investment opportunities available to institutional investors and provide additional sources of return. However, their use introduces risks that must be carefully assessed, including the performance of the referenced asset and the creditworthiness of the institution providing the investment solution. Equity-Linked Deposits Let us examine Equity-Linked Deposits. These are investment vehicles that track assets beyond traditional fixed income, such as equities. They are becoming increasingly common in the region, particularly in East and Southern Africa, where institutional clients seek returns associated with the performance of equity markets and equity derivatives. Generally, these products combine a deposit with an equity call option. The return enhancement is derived from the performance of the call option acquired by the investor. The option may reference the shares of a single company, an equity index or a basket of equities, such as the MSCI World Index or the S&P 500 Index. The investor places funds in the deposit and receives the principal at maturity, subject to the terms of the structure and the creditworthiness of the issuing institution. The call option provides the potential for an additional return if the referenced equity or index performs favourably over the investment period. This structure allows investors to participate in equity market performance without purchasing the underlying shares directly. It may therefore appeal to investors seeking exposure to international equities while retaining a deposit-based investment structure. The solution can also be customised to reflect the investor’s preferred market exposure, investment horizon and return objectives. An investor may select a single equity where there is a specific market view or choose a broad index or basket to diversify exposure across several companies, sectors or markets. Furthermore, by using a cross-currency swap as an overlay, the structure can be converted into payouts in the local currency. This can allow the investor to receive returns in a currency aligned with its liabilities or investment requirements. Depending on market conditions and the design of the structure, the currency component may also contribute to the overall yield enhancement. As with the other derivative-based investment strategies discussed in this series, counterparty credit risk remains an important consideration. The investor relies on the institution offering the solution, often a bank, to fulfil its payment obligations. The creditworthiness of the issuer must therefore be considered alongside the potential performance of the referenced equity or index. Credit-Linked Deposits Another yield-enhancement strategy is the Credit-Linked Deposit. This product may be particularly relevant to investors in our region because of their familiarity with government and corporate bonds. A Credit-Linked Deposit allows an investor to gain exposure to a sovereign or major corporation without holding the underlying security directly. It can provide customised coupon payments similar to those that the investor might receive from owning the referenced bond. The structure can be created by combining a deposit with a Credit Default Swap, thereby creating a funded credit exposure. The investor selects a reference entity based on its risk appetite and receives a corresponding return. A reference entity with a lower perceived probability of default would generally offer a smaller coupon, while exposure to a higher-risk name may provide a larger coupon to compensate for the additional credit risk. The payment profile can also be customised. Instead of receiving the semi-annual coupon payments commonly associated with bonds, for example, an investor may structure the Credit-Linked Deposit to make quarterly payments. This flexibility can assist institutional investors in managing cash flows and matching investment income against expected liabilities. A distinctive feature of the Credit-Linked Deposit is that it removes the need for the investor to purchase the referenced bond or open a securities depository account in the issuer’s country. This may reduce administrative requirements and eliminate some of the custody or depositary fees associated with direct ownership. For illustration, an investor in Ghana seeking exposure to the Kenyan sovereign could obtain that exposure without establishing accounts or a securities depository arrangement in Kenya. Instead, the investor could engage a suitable counterparty, preferably a bank, place an amount corresponding to the desired sovereign exposure and enter into a credit derivative referencing that sovereign. Under this arrangement, the investor obtains synthetic exposure to the referenced sovereign. The deposit and the credit component together generate the return sought by the investor. The structure does not eliminate credit risk. If a credit event occurs in relation to the referenced entity, the investor may lose part or all of the amount invested, depending on the terms of the product and the recovery value of the referenced obligation. Since the Credit-Linked Deposit is an over-the-counter structure, the investor is also exposed to the creditworthiness of the counterparty with which the transaction is executed. If that counterparty becomes insolvent or is otherwise unable to meet its obligations, the investor may suffer a loss independently of the performance of the referenced sovereign or corporation. Investors must therefore assess both the reference entity and the institution providing the structure. Regulatory Considerations and Market Opportunity Implementing these yield-enhancement strategies requires careful consideration of the applicable local regulations. Certain structures may fall within the alternative investment provisions under the Guidelines for Asset Managers and the Guidelines on Investment of Tier 2 and Tier 3 Pension Scheme Funds. Where a structure provides exposure to an asset or reference entity outside Ghana, it may also be treated as an external investment. Investors must therefore consider the applicable asset-allocation limits, approval requirements and foreign-currency rules before entering into a transaction. The foreign-currency component of these investments may require compliance with guidance issued by the Bank of Ghana. Pension funds, asset managers and other institutional investors must also ensure that any proposed investment is permitted under their governing mandates and internal investment policies. These requirements do not remove the potential value of the structures. They establish the conditions within which the investments must be assessed and implemented. Regulatory limits can restrict the proportion of a portfolio allocated to external or alternative investments, thereby containing the overall exposure of a fund to these instruments. For asset managers, pension funds and corporates, the potential opportunity lies in using permitted allocations more effectively to achieve diversification and pursue enhanced returns. Equity-Linked Deposits can provide access to international equity performance, while Credit-Linked Deposits can provide exposure to sovereign or corporate credit without requiring direct ownership of the referenced securities. Cash flows generated by these investments, including coupons or investment proceeds, may eventually be repatriated and converted into local currency. Investors must therefore consider not only the prospective return but also currency movements, repatriation requirements and the effect of the investment on their regulatory asset-allocation limits. A depreciation of the local currency, for instance, may increase the local-currency value of a foreign-currency investment and affect the proportion of the portfolio allocated to external assets. The investor may consequently need to rebalance the portfolio to remain within the applicable limits. The suitability of these solutions will depend on each investor’s mandate, risk appetite, liquidity requirements and capacity to evaluate structured investments. Their adoption must therefore be supported by appropriate governance, transparent documentation and a clear understanding of the underlying market and credit exposures. Conclusion Derivatives are widely used to manage market risk, but their application extends beyond hedging. Equity-Linked Deposits and Credit-Linked Deposits demonstrate how derivative-based structures can help institutional investors access new markets, diversify their portfolios and pursue additional returns without necessarily purchasing the underlying securities directly. These benefits must be considered alongside the relevant risks. Equity-linked structures depend on the performance of the referenced shares or indices, while Credit-Linked Deposits expose investors to the credit risk of the reference entity. Both also create exposure to the institution providing the investment solution. The development of these products will require engagement among investors, financial institutions and regulators. Investors need sufficient expertise and governance arrangements to evaluate the structures, while providers must ensure that the products are transparent, suitable and properly understood. Regulators also have an important role in establishing the conditions under which innovation can take place without compromising the protection of investors or the stability of the market. Used within appropriate regulatory and investment limits, structured solutions can broaden the range of opportunities available to local institutional investors and contribute to the continued development of Ghana’s financial market. ****** Gerald Nana Kusi is the Head, Institutional Sales and Structuring, Absa Bank Ghana LTD

items.title: 2027: Security tops as APC-PCC unveils 4-point manifesto
items.description: By Soni Daniel, Emma Ujah & Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA—The Presidency yesterday asked Nigerians to study the past and current manifestoes of the All Progressives Congress, APC, and judge the party by the promises it has kept since 2023 when it assumed power. Read Also: Security of lives and property to top Tinubu’s agenda in 2nd term – APC The Presidential Campaign Council, APC-PCC, also said President Bola Tinubu will pay priority attention to protection of lives and property if he wins the presidential election on January 16, 2027. Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila, who made the declaration at the unveiling of the APC manifesto, titled ‘’From Reforms to Prosperity,’’ described the manifesto as a binding pact with the electorate. “A manifesto, in its strictest sense, is simply a contract between the people and their leaders. It is an inviolable contract, and we take the strict interpretation of what a manifesto represents as gospel under this administration,” he said. He admitted that the reforms had put real pressure on households, adding that the people living through it deserve to be heard. “Nobody should have to pretend that life is easy at the moment,” he said. The former House of Representatives’ Speaker, nonetheless, defended President Tinubu’s decision to act, saying the President confronted the subsidy burden and a distorted foreign exchange system when he took responsibility for the country in 2023. He said: “Leaving those problems untouched would have continued to weaken our ability to invest in the future. The difference between a politician and a leader is that while a politician thinks about the next election, a leader thinks about the next generation. And that is exactly what President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has demonstrated. Four pillars The manifesto rests on four pillars, including a secure and resilient nation; a better quality and more affordable life for every Nigerian; energy, infrastructure and economic growth; and effective and accountable governance. They are tied to the eight priority areas of the Renewed Hope Agenda, which the document said would be carried out on four foundations – macroeconomic stability; the rule of law; institutional capability; and national cohesion. By 2031, the document commits to power generation scaled towards 10,000 megawatts, annual economic growth of six per cent, and youth unemployment and out-of-school children, both halved. It also promises 20,000 additional teachers and health insurance expanded from more than 23 million enrollees to 40 per cent of Nigerians. Primary health centres will function in at least 90 per cent of facilities, up from the current 53 per cent. It further promises to work towards 200,000 homes under the Tinubu Mass Social Housing Scheme, Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria, FMBN, mortgages and licensed private developers, tracked on a public dashboard. Gbajabiamila added that the document had committed the government to installing seven million additional electricity meters. He said it would also expose the government’s own record to public inspection, noting that “the manifesto commits us to publishing targets, identifying those responsible and reporting progress to the public. Citizens should be able to see where delivery is succeeding and where it is falling short.’’ Gbajabiamila, who said the party would ask for the electorate’s mandate in 2027 and earn it, stated: “A party asking to continue in government must be prepared to answer to the people whose mandate it seeks. “The child studying tonight should have a fair chance of becoming the professional he/she hopes to be. The man opening his workshop tomorrow should be able to grow beyond the struggle to keep it open. Their ambitions deserve a country organised to help them succeed.’’ In his remarks, the Minister of Budget and Economic Planning, Atiku Bagudu, who chaired the APC 2027 Manifesto Unveiling Committee, said the administration had made progress but noted that more remained to be done. He cited the last Nigerian Economic Summit, where he said the private sector acknowledged that the President had delivered on his promises. “But, as we all know, even before anybody tells him, Mr President acknowledges that we have done well. However, until we deliver and ensure that every Nigerian feels the impact of prosperity, especially hardworking Nigerians and those who need support, we still have work to do,” Bagudu said. He recalled how Tinubu, during his campaign in Zamfara State, directed a State House official to give money to a struggling carrot seller, citing it as evidence of the President’s concern for ordinary Nigerians. “So, Mr President, without being influenced by any outsider, said we should confront our reality and address these challenges. As I have said, he was not concerned about the next election but about prosperity,” Bagudu said. No leader has transformed Nigeria like Tinubu Spokesperson of APC Presidential Campaign Council, PCC, and Minister of Solid Minerals, Dele Alake, said the President removed fuel subsidy and unified the foreign exchange market at a political cost to himself. “Regardless of the political consequences, or even the President’s own political situation and aspirations, he carried out genuine structural reforms,” he said. Alake, who alleged that powerful interests had exploited the subsidy regime and were resisting its removal, said: “It takes a man of courage, a man of grit, brains and brawn, to withstand the pressure of the cabal, which would fight back, and they are fighting back over the removal of fuel subsidy.’’ On the exchange rate, he alleged that some people with connections to the Central Bank of Nigeria, CBN, or top government officials obtained millions of dollars at the official rate. “In the twinkle of an eye, they would become billionaires while sitting in their backyards, making no contribution to production in the economy to shore up the naira. And, of course, the result, as you all knew, was a free fall,” he said. Tinubu has given 1.6m Nigerians opportunity to attend varsity—Idris The Minister of Information, Mohammed Idris, answered critics who said only a few Nigerians benefitted from the reforms. “When the road between Abuja and Kano is being constructed, I am not aware that anybody needs to show his ID card to prove that he belongs to the APC, is a rich man or belongs to a particular class before he can use it,” he said. On security, he said travellers on the Abuja-Kaduna road no longer have to ask whether bandits were still operating there. “Today, nobody asks such questions. You take your car from here to Kano without asking whether terrorists, bandits, kidnappers or whoever was operating along the road is still there. This was not the situation before,” he said. On NELFUND, the minister stated: “So, if you are looking for an example of Nigerians benefiting from these reforms, the 1.6 million young men and women and their parents are there. Nobody asks questions about their political affiliation.’’ Idris added that the Financial Action Task Force, FATF, had delisted Nigeria from its grey list, adding that headline and food inflation were both declining. “That is why we are saying today that, yes, we have laid the foundation for reforms, and we are progressively moving towards a period of prosperity. As I said, by 2031, it will be almost impossible for anybody to reverse this course,” he said. While appealing to the media, the minister said: “You do not have to like the administration of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. You do not have to like him, but all of us must like Nigeria.’’ The APC-PCC also said on the occasion that President Bola Tinubu would pay priority attention to the protection of lives and property if he won the forthcoming presidential election on January 16, 2027. To achieve that objective, the party has promised to recruit 28,000 additional military personnel and 50,000 police officers, in order to strengthen Nigeria’s security architecture. On her part, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Dr. Jumoke Oduwole, who is the Deputy Director, Directorate of Manifesto and Policy Development of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, made the declaration. The council also promised to complete the establishment and equipping of the four new Army Divisions in Makurdi, Ilorin, Jalingo and Benin City; sustain intelligence-led kinetic operations against insurgents and kidnapping networks to degrade and dismantle their operating bases. In order to deal with kidnappers who have turned the nation’s forests into criminal hideouts, the ruling party promised to deploy trained Forest Guards, Agro-Rangers and Mining Marshals to safeguard agricultural belts, farming communities, grazing routes, national forest reserves and mineral deposits. The minister said the APC administration planned to make Nigeria a fortress where everyone would live happily to actualize their potentials without any form of fear. Vanguard News The post 2027: Security tops as APC-PCC unveils 4-point manifesto appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: JoyNews’ Emmanuel Dzivenu named finalist for West Africa journalism excellence award
items.description: JoyNews journalist and television producer Emmanuel Dzivenu has been named a finalist in the 2026 Excellence in Journalism Awards organised by the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID). His documentary, “Leukaemia: Last Chance Abroad – Agony of Ghanaians Diagnosed with Blood Cancer,” is among 17 entries shortlisted from 424 submissions by 277 journalists across nine West African countries. The documentary exposes the struggles of Ghanaians diagnosed with leukaemia who are forced to raise huge sums of money to seek life-saving bone marrow transplants abroad, often losing precious treatment time in the process. It highlights the limited access to specialised transplant services for leukaemia in Ghana and across West Africa, which leaves patients seeking treatment overseas, including in South Africa. Beyond the struggles of affected families, the investigation argues for establishing a Centre for Haematology and Clinical Genetics in Ghana that could serve patients across the subregion and reduce dependence on treatment abroad. Rigorous and competitive selection process Mr Dzivenu’s recognition follows a highly competitive selection process involving hundreds of submissions from journalists across West Africa. According to CJID, the 2026 awards attracted 424 entries from 277 journalists , representing a 54.2 per cent increase over the 275 entries received in 2025. The submissions came from nine countries: Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal, The Gambia, Sierra Leone, Côte d’Ivoire, Liberia, Guinea and Benin. The entries underwent an initial screening, after which the five highest-ranked submissions in each of the eight award categories advanced to the next stage. An independent panel of six accomplished journalists from across the region then subjected the selected entries to further scrutiny. Hannah Ajakaiye, founding editor of FactsMatter NG, chaired the jury, which also included Manasseh Azure Awuni , a multiple award-winning Ghanaian investigative journalist and editor. Other members were Maxime Domegni , an award-winning journalist and Francophone Africa Editor for the Global Investigative Journalism Network; Ajibola Amzat , Africa Editor at the Centre for Collaborative Investigative Journalism; Kent Mensah , Chief Ghana Correspondent for The Africa Report; and Amaka Okoye , Bureau Chief for Deutsche Welle’s Studio Lagos in Nigeria. Each judge independently assessed the entries for accuracy, fairness, originality, innovation, depth of research, quality of writing, public significance, and adherence to ethical standards. The judges subsequently deliberated to select entries that demonstrated a strong combination of compelling storytelling and rigorous journalism. The process produced 17 finalist entries across eight categories, including Health Reporting, Community Reporting, Human Rights Reporting, Social Accountability, Climate Change Reporting, Solutions Journalism, Fact-Checking, and Sexual and Gender-Based Violence. The shortlisted works cover investigations into suspected killings in Ghanaian police custody, illegal rosewood trafficking, cross-border gold exploitation, environmental pollution, human rights abuses and healthcare challenges across the region. Jury chair Hannah Ajakaiye praised the quality of submissions, particularly reporting on social accountability, environmental issues and human rights. “This year’s entries showed particular strength in reporting on social accountability, the environment and human rights,” she said. CJID Chief Executive Officer Dapo Olorunyomi congratulated the finalists and commended journalists across West Africa for pursuing stories of public interest despite difficult working conditions and limited resources. “The stories recognised this year reflect the courage, persistence and public service that sustain journalism in West Africa,” he said. Winners to be announced in Abuja The finalists will be honoured at an awards ceremony on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, at the Abuja Continental Hotel in Nigeria , as part of the Media and Development Conference. The ceremony will announce winners and runners-up in each of the eight categories. The Royal Norwegian Embassy in Abuja and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of the Netherlands support the 2026 awards. The Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development is a leading West African media innovation organisation dedicated to strengthening investigative journalism, promoting media freedom, advancing digital rights and fostering democratic accountability across the continent.

items.title: Gates Foundation says AGRA’s revised transformation strategy is strengthening Africa’s food systems
items.description: The Gates Foundation says AGRA’s revised strategy for transforming Africa’s food systems, which prioritises country-level needs and better connects farmers to markets, is helping strengthen the agrifood sector. Director of Economic Opportunity for Africa at the Gates Foundation, Enock Chikava, says over the past two decades, AGRA and its partners have helped build key components of the agricultural system that African farmers depend on to succeed. “By supporting about 35,000 agro dealers and 118 African seed companies—helping bring more than 650 improved seed varieties to market—they have expanded the capacity to develop and supply seeds that can help farmers improve their harvests,” he observes. Established in 2006 with former Ghanaian UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan as its first board chair, AGRA is a pan-African institution focused on scaling agricultural innovations that help small-scale farming enterprises increase incomes, improve livelihoods, and enhance food security. In an article on the website of the Gates Foundation reflecting on AGRA’s work over the last 20 years, Mr Chikava notes that AGRA’s “investments in agricultural research, advisory services and access to inputs have also helped build the infrastructure farmers need to make better decisions, increase productivity and earn more from their land.” “These are important foundations for a more productive and prosperous agricultural sector,” he said . Mr Chikava observes that the challenges facing farmers across sub-Saharan Africa are immense, and no single organisation or approach can address them all. Crop yields in sub-Saharan Africa are half those in India and one-fifth those in the United States, reflecting significant constraints on soil quality and productivity. Climate-driven extreme weather, El Niño, conflict and fertiliser price shocks linked to the Iran crisis are adding further pressure. The Hormuz blockade alone disrupted around a third of global fertiliser exports. Scientific assessments also warn that a 2°C rise in global temperatures could reduce crop yields in sub-Saharan Africa by about 10 per cent, he said. Missed goals and the future of African agriculture The Gates Foundation official recalls that when AGRA was established in 2006, it set ambitious goals for 2020 such as doubling productivity and incomes for 20 million smallholder households and halving hunger and food insecurity across 20 countries. “These goals were not met, and civil society organisations have urged accountability for this failure. We agree. As a longtime funder, we share responsibility. Hunger across Africa remains unacceptably high, and progress in agricultural productivity has not translated into the improved food security and farmer incomes that are needed.” He, however, says the Foundation has continued to fund AGRA because of the change in strategy. “Following a 2022 evaluation that found mixed outcomes for farmers, AGRA adjusted its strategy. We continued investing because its new approach was more closely aligned with countries’ own priorities and placed greater emphasis on connecting farmers to finance and markets,” he said. “But continued investment cannot mean business as usual. It must mean learning from what fell short, listening to farmers, governments, civil society, and critics, and being willing to change course. Our responsibility is not simply to stay committed to African agriculture, but to ensure our investments deliver better results for the farmers and families they are intended to serve. We remain committed to that work for the long haul.” AGRA President Alice Ruhweza has previously assured that the institution continues to learn from previous experiences. “We have learned that distributing seeds and fertiliser, while necessary, was never going to be sufficient on its own.” “The harder, longer work is in building systems that hold together under pressure: linking climate adaptation to market development, connecting public investment to private sector participation, and helping governments strengthen the institutions that turn strategies into results.” Achieving ambitions will take time Mr Chikava notes that although hunger has not declined and farmer incomes remain too low, since 2005, cereal yields across Africa have risen by about 40 per cent, and farm output has nearly doubled in real terms. He says the realities of farming across sub-Saharan Africa are complex, and there is no single path to growth and prosperity. “Our foundation’s approach is to back governments’ own agricultural development plans and give farmers the options and support they need to increase productivity and grow their incomes.” Mr Chikava assures that despite different perspectives on how best to advance African agriculture, the Gates Foundation shares important ambitions with other organisations and partners. These include reducing dependence on imported inputs, making African countries less vulnerable to global price shocks, and creating more prosperous farming communities. “Achieving these ambitions will take time and sustained effort, particularly given the many pressures facing farmers. We welcome more partners, ideas and solutions, and take calls for greater accountability seriously,” he said. “By working together, we can help farming families across Africa increase their incomes and build lasting prosperity,” Mr Chikava concluded.

items.title: José Luis Pontón, ingeniero informático: “Una IA que entiende el movimiento humano puede aprender a imitar a una persona y suplantarla”
items.description: La afición a los videojuegos y las amistades en entornos digitales llevaron al ingeniero informático José Luis Pontón (Barcelona, 28 años) a dedicar su investigación posdoctoral a la realidad virtual, la robótica y la inteligencia artificial. “A mí me gustaba crear. Creo que los videojuegos te permiten crear mundos y cosas que en el mundo real no puedes hacer”, asegura el desarrollador de software , galardonado en la última edición de los premios de la Sociedad Científica Informática de España (SCIE) y la Fundación BBVA , en la categoría Investigadores Jóvenes en Informática, por sus avances en realidad virtual. Pontón atiende a EL PAÍS antes de regresar a Alemania, donde trabaja en el Max Planck Institute for Informatics, en Saarbrücken. Allí elabora, junto a otros investigadores, una herramienta que reconstruiye el movimiento humano a partir de datos captados por sensores y trasladarlo a entornos de realidad virtual mediante avatares digitales. La tecnología permitiría, según Pontón, mantener videollamadas en las que los avatares reprodujeran el lenguaje corporal de los participantes en tiempo real, como si compartieran un mismo espacio virtual. Seguir leyendo

items.title: “El ‘cringe’ se ha cargado internet”: por qué los jóvenes ya no quieren subir nada a las redes
items.description: “Tengo la sensación de que el cringe se ha cargado las redes sociales”, asegura Toni Hernández, estudiante de diseño nacido en 2007. “Recuerdo que cuando tenía 9 o 10 años consumía youtubers que hablaban de videojuegos, novelas visuales o anime . Aquellos creadores tenían una forma de expresarse con más carácter, eran más divertidos, gesticulaban mucho… Y hoy se les consideraría frikis”. Hernández es muy joven y, sin embargo, ya siente nostalgia de unas redes en las que cada publicación no implicaba —como desde hace unos años sucede para él, para sus coetáneos y para sus referentes online— enfrentarse y sortear un abismo: el abismo del cringe. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Pesadilla en el duelo: encontrar a la expareja en una aplicación de citas
items.description: Isabel Díaz Ayuso asegura que en Madrid es prácticamente imposible que alguien se encuentre con su expareja. Más allá de la veracidad de sus palabras, donde es muy factible encontrarse con un ex es un a aplicación de citas . Precisamente eso es lo que ocurre en la nueva temporada de la serie de Netflix Nadie quiere esto , donde dos de sus personajes, tras romper, se encuentran en una aplicación de citas. Quien haya pasado por esa situación sabe bien lo demoledor que es, y el equipo de Tinder, consciente de ello, permite bloquear contactos específicos. Aunque no es específicamente para bloquear a exparejas, sin duda funciona como un poderoso, y útil, modo anti-ex. Un estudio realizado por la aplicación señala que el 40% de los usuarios se ha encontrado con su una antigua relación en la aplicación. “Puede que no podamos evitarte encuentros incómodos en la cafetería, pero sí podemos darte un mayor control sobre tu experiencia en Tinder”, dice Bernadette Morgan, directora de producto del área de Confianza y Seguridad de la aplicación, sobre la función ‘bloquear contactos’. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El debate | ¿Es ‘La bola negra’ una obra maestra?
items.description: Desde su estreno, La bola negra ha sido recibida como uno de los grandes acontecimientos del cine español reciente. Inspirada en la obra inacabada de Federico García Lorca, la película entrelaza varias historias sobre el deseo, la memoria y la represión a lo largo de distintas épocas de la historia de España. Su éxito de crítica, sus premios internacionales y su impacto cultural reflejan la gran acogida que ha tenido entre el público. Pero también hay quien cuestiona algunos aspectos de su ambición narrativa y su ejecución y muestran escaso entusiasmo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: “Chepibe”, “asegunes”, “medalaganario”. Palabras estelares
items.description: El momento estelar del acto en que se presentó la nueva edición del Diccionario de la lengua española, el 30 de octubre, llegó cuando los directores o presidentes de las 22 academias de América, Filipinas y Guinea se fueron poniendo de pie sucesivamente en las primeras filas de la repleta sala y, dotados de micrófono de diadema, cada uno explicó una palabra de entre las que había aportado su institución a la obra común. De pronto, se hicieron visibles la riqueza del idioma español, su pluralidad de influencias; la imaginación de los hablantes para nombrar las realidades propias y también las compartidas. Seguir leyendo

items.description: Los inmigrantes llegan a España con más salud ―como promedio― que una persona nacional de su misma edad y sexo. Pero “ venden su salud para mandar dinero a sus familias”, en palabras de Luis Andrés Gimeno Feliu, médico de familia y profesor de la Universidad de Zaragoza. La ventaja de la que parten los que no han llegado a través de rutas peligrosas o violencia se va perdiendo por culpa de los empleos precarios, malas condiciones de la vivienda, pocos recursos para un buen estilo de vida, las dificultades para acceder a la sanidad o incluso el racismo. items.title: Canarias se suma al aviso rojo por ‘Bruna’ y ‘Charles’, que persiste en Extremadura y Castilla y León
items.description: Los borrascas Bruna y Charles no se suman a la huelga general convocada para este miércoles. Muy al contrario, han unido sus fuerzas para azotar a España con el “día más adverso” del temporal de lluvias persistentes y abundantes, fuertes vientos y mala mar que comenzó el sábado y que aún durará hasta el jueves. Entre las dos, han llenado de avisos el mapa de la Agencia Estatal de Meteorología (Aemet), que los ha decretado en 14 comunidades más Ceuta , todo el país salvo Asturias, Cantabria, Baleares y Melilla. items.title: La Junta andaluza desvía a otras partidas los fondos para depurar aguas a pesar de las multas millonarias de la UE por vertidos
items.description: El canon del agua en Andalucía, que cada usuario paga cada mes en su factura y que se ideó para financiar la deficiente depuración, se ha convertido en un juego del trilero. Los gobiernos socialistas en la Junta de Andalucía y los posteriores del PP lo han recaudado, pero no lo han invertido. El primer Ejecutivo de Juan Manuel Moreno Bonilla (PP) lo derogó en 2022 tras calificarlo de “fraude” y lo reimplantó al año siguiente un 30% más caro. El pasado ejercicio lo destinó a reparaciones de daños por las intensas lluvias. En 2027, el Presupuesto prevé dedicar los fondos a otras obras hidráulicas, a pesar de que la falta de depuración ha costado 84.772.670 euros en multas desde 2018 y la cifra total ascenderá a 100 millones al finalizar esta década. items.title: Los interrogantes de la ‘Operación Luna’: qué se sabe y qué no sobre la presunta venta de menores
items.description: Vivían puerta con puerta, pero no sabían su nombre. Cuando a primera hora del miércoles los furgones policiales cortaron la calle, los vecinos de la localidad de Montijo (15.195 habitantes, Badajoz) intuyeron que el operativo iba a la casa de fachada ocre y molduras destartaladas. Acertaron. Presintieron también que el registro tenía algo que ver con el tráfico de drogas. Que se equivocaban lo supieron cuando, como les ordenaron los agentes, regresaron a sus domicilios y la noticia de lo que ocurría en ese instante al otro lado de la calle les estalló en sus teléfonos. “Desarticulan una red criminal de tráfico y compraventa de bebés”. Una sinfonía de notificaciones, de titulares perturbadores que comenzaron a darle dimensiones pesadillescas a lo que pasaba en la casa de su vecina sin nombre. Seguir leyendo

Sus integrantes están en campaña para que se prohíba el uso del uniforme escolar en la pornografía y para que deje de promocionarse como un disfraz erótico. items.title: Dangote Cement shelves London listing, blames market conditions for blow to LSE
items.description: Nigeria’s Dangote Cement postponed its plans for a secondary listing in London on Tuesday, citing deteriorating market conditions, in a setback for the UK bourse. The decision came after market volatility following the US midterm elections , but the company may revisit the plan to list in London when conditions are more stable, a person with knowledge of the situation said. Wall Street tumbled last week after the Democrats’ midterm victory deepened investor concerns about whether the AI boom can last, with London’s benchmark FTSE 100 index also ending the week lower. Dangote Cement, which listed on the Nigerian stock market in 2010, said in May it ​was in early talks over a potential London listing , a move that would have widened its access to overseas investors and capital. It has floated the idea of a London listing several times over 15 years, but global downturns and the COVID-19 pandemic have ​derailed its attempts. It is part of the sprawling business empire of Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote, who launched ​Africa’s biggest share sale yet in September with the initial public offering of his oil refinery. Dangote Cement’s board of directors, which met ‌on ⁠Tuesday, made the decision not to proceed with the listing plans in light of current market conditions and the firm’s strategic priorities, it said in a statement. “These are pretty awful conditions for anyone to attempt an IPO,” said Samuel Kerr, an analyst at M&A analytics platform Mergermarket, pointing to the recent rise in equity ​volatility. “Dangote could probably do a ​deal now, but if ⁠it has the option of waiting for a better market, that would probably result in a better outcome and perhaps a higher valuation.” NO EFFECT ON BUSINESS ​PLANS A growing number of companies have either abandoned the London bourse or been bought ​out by larger ⁠rivals or private equity firms, while the IPO market has remained subdued. African mobile money service Airtel Money, which made its London debut last month, has largely traded around its IPO price of £1.96 ($2.64) a share since its listing. The cement company, which has a market valuation of 24.79 trillion naira ($18.4 billion), said its shares remain listed on the Nigerian bourse and that the decision does not affect its operations or business plans.

items.title: Cedi strengthens on GoldBod’s boost to forex liquidity; going for GH¢12.15 against a dollar at forex bureaus
items.description: The Ghana cedi strengthened against the US dollar over the past two weeks, following Goldbod’s support for the foreign exchange market. The local currency clawed back gains on sustained forex supply from GoldBod’s spot auctions. It improved modestly in the interbank market while remaining relatively stable in the retail market. In the interbank market, the cedi appreciated by 0.09%, 0.14% and 0.50% against the US dollar, the pound sterling and the euro. It traded at GH¢11.64 against the US dollar, GH¢15.55 against the pound and GH¢12.98 against the euro, respectively. In the retail market, the dollar and euro exchange rates remained unchanged at GH¢12.08 and GH¢ 13.60. However, it depreciated against the pound by 0.63% to GH¢16.00the dollar. On a month-on-month basis, the cedi’s year-to-date depreciation narrowed by 0.69 percentage points to 10.07% at the end of October 2026, down from 10.76% in September 2026. “We believe October’s US$1.011 billion intermediation, offered at a uniform market-clearing rate, significantly anchored demand expectations and guided market pricing”, said Databank Research. “Looking ahead, our forecast points to a modest appreciation toward GH¢11.41 to a dollar by the end of the next fortnight, despite impending seasonal import demand pressures. With US$800 million earmarked for commercial bank auctions from a US$1.2 billion November 2026 gross intermediation, we expect sustained dollar liquidity to support near-term exchange rate stability”, it added. Meanwhile, the cedi began the week going for GH¢12.15 against the US dollar at the forex bureaus.

items.title: Visa For Music 2026 : Rabat s’apprête à accueillir la scène musicale africaine
items.description: Rabat s’apprête à vibrer au rythme des musiques d’Afrique et du Moyen-Orient. Du 18 au 21 novembre 2026, la capitale accueillera la 13ᵉ édition de Visa For Music, festival et marché professionnel dédié aux musiques du continent africain et de la région du Moyen-Orient. Pendant quatre jours, la manifestation réunira 500 artistes et près de 1 000 professionnels marocains et internationaux, avec une programmation répartie entre quatre scènes de la capitale et un important volet professionnel consacré aux enjeux de l’industrie musicale. Le coup d’envoi sera donné mercredi 18 novembre avec une parade urbaine, avant une cérémonie d’ouverture au Théâtre National Mohammed V. Le public pourra ensuite assister à des dizaines de showcases répartis entre quatre espaces : le Théâtre National Mohammed V, la Salle Bahnini, l’Institut National Supérieur de Musique et des Arts Chorégraphiques (INSMAC) et la scène du Chellah, dédiée aux musiques électroniques. Cette édition entend mettre en avant la diversité des scènes musicales internationales, avec des artistes venus notamment de Belgique, du Congo, de l’Inde, d’Haïti, du Sénégal, d’Italie, du Canada, de Tunisie ou encore d’Afrique du Sud. Parmi les artistes programmés figurent notamment Siân Pottok, Erol Josué, Mariaa Siga, Enzo Avitabile, Moonshine ou encore Taroug. La scène marocaine au cœur de la programmation La création marocaine et sa diaspora occupent également une place importante dans cette édition. Les showcases mettront notamment à l’honneur Meryem Aboulouafa, Sara Moullablad ainsi que le projet électro Gnawatronic, porté par Omary & Hind Ennaira. Le Focus Maroc réunira pour sa part quatre projets de la scène nationale : R2D, JBIINA, ONZY JAZZBAR et YVZID. Cette présence s’inscrit dans la volonté du festival de favoriser la visibilité des artistes marocains et leur accès aux réseaux professionnels internationaux. Un marché pour les professionnels de l’industrie musicale Au-delà des concerts, Visa For Music se veut également un véritable espace de rencontres et de développement professionnel. Artistes, producteurs, programmateurs, labels, agences de booking et institutions sont attendus autour d’un Forum, d’un salon professionnel réunissant plus de 30 exposants et de rendez-vous B2B. Des sessions de speed meetings permettront notamment aux artistes et à leurs équipes de présenter leurs projets à des programmateurs et d’explorer de nouvelles possibilités de diffusion et de tournée. Le Forum abordera plusieurs problématiques qui traversent actuellement l’industrie musicale, notamment la circulation des artistes, le rôle des festivals dans les territoires, l’accès aux marchés internationaux et l’impact croissant de l’intelligence artificielle sur la création. Parmi les rendez-vous annoncés figurent notamment les conférences « Entre authenticité et tendances : la création musicale à l’ère des algorithmes » et « Des scènes locales aux marchés européens : construire une tournée internationale ». L’intelligence artificielle au cœur des échanges La technologie occupera une place importante dans cette édition, avec des ateliers consacrés notamment à la production musicale et à l’utilisation de l’intelligence artificielle sur Ableton Live. Les professionnels pourront également travailler sur la présentation de leurs projets à l’international, leur identité artistique et leur présence scénique. Des masterclasses porteront par ailleurs sur les stratégies de diffusion et de distribution, ainsi que sur la structuration des industries musicales africaines, avec notamment un focus consacré au cas du Cameroun. Une édition tournée vers l’international Avec plus de 900 candidatures reçues depuis 92 pays, Visa For Music confirme son positionnement comme plateforme de découverte, de rencontre et de circulation des artistes. L’édition 2026 réunira au total 40 projets artistiques, dont quatre formations participant à la parade urbaine. Le festival prévoit également un programme OFF destiné à prolonger les échanges autour de sujets comme la découvrabilité des artistes et la circulation de la musique sur les marchés professionnels africains. Depuis sa création, Visa For Music revendique également une démarche en faveur de la jeunesse, de la diversité et de la représentation féminine. L’accès aux activités est notamment gratuit pour les jeunes professionnels marocains et de la diaspora, tandis que des tarifs étudiants et des actions de médiation culturelle sont proposés. Du 18 au 21 novembre, Rabat s’imposera ainsi comme un point de rencontre entre création artistique, industrie musicale et échanges internationaux, avec une ambition affichée : renforcer la circulation des talents africains et leur présence sur les scènes internationales. The post Visa For Music 2026 : Rabat s’apprête à accueillir la scène musicale africaine appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.description: Nigeria’s upstream oil regulator has approved ​145 new well-drilling operations, 595 well re-entries and ‌39 field development plans (FDPs) so far this year as it seeks to boost crude output, attract investment and strengthen ​energy security, a senior official said on ​Tuesday. The Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) said ⁠the approvals reflected faster regulatory processing that has ​reduced project delays and costs for operators “Year to date, ​about 39 FDPs have been approved. About 145 new well-drilling approvals granted. Year to date, about 595 well re-entry approvals ​were granted,” NUPRC Chief Executive Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan said ​at an oil conference in Lagos Eyesan, represented by Ahmad Abdullahi, ‌deputy ⁠director of basin administration, said faster approvals were helping operators advance projects needed to meet production targets and support energy availability She said Nigeria had more ​than 100 drilling ​rigs, with ⁠46 active this year, up more than 300% from 2021 levels Eyesan also said ​seismic companies had invested more than $100 ​million ⁠in Nigeria since the Petroleum Industry Act came into force three years ago, improving exploration data and supporting ⁠efforts ​to discover new oil and ​gas reserves The regulator is also working to curb crude theft across ​the country

items.title: Congo’s Ebola cases surpass 11,000, government data show
items.description: The number of confirmed Ebola cases in ​the Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed ‌11,000, government data showed on Tuesday. Confirmed infections now total 11,042, and 5,387 people have died, ​the data showed The outbreak, caused ​by the rare Bundibugyo species of the ⁠Ebola virus, was declared in mid-May. ​There are no approved treatments or vaccines ​for this species It is the second-largest and deadliest outbreak on record behind only the 2014-2016 West ​African outbreak, which infected more than ​28,600 people and killed more than 11,000 Eight of ‌Congo’s ⁠26 provinces have been affected, and many deaths have occurred outside treatment centres Delayed detection, conflict and strained health services have ​led to ​a more ⁠rapid spread of the virus than in previous outbreaks The disease ​has now been reported in East , ​Central ⁠and West Africa , giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the ⁠continent ​to date

Oil rises from two-month low as Hormuz shipping attacks offset Iran truce hopes
items.description: Oil prices rose on Wednesday after falling to two-month lows in the previous session, as the market swung between hopes for a de-escalation in the Iran ​war and concerns about ongoing attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent ‌futures climbed 71 cents, or 0.78%, to $92.20 a barrel by 0119 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose 49 cents, or 0.57%, to $86.53. New data showed that 37 ships were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz and ​surrounding waterways in October, the highest monthly total since the start of the war, ​according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. And 10 attacks ⁠have been recorded so far in November. Videos posted on social media on Sunday and verified ​by Reuters showed a Navig8 tanker on fire near the coast of Oman, one of three ​tankers hit on Sunday for using “unauthorised routes” through the strait, according to the Iranian state broadcaster. Another tanker was struck northeast of Oman’s Lima, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Tuesday. Iran’s Revolutionary ​Guards Navy said in a separate statement on Tuesday that two tankers caught fire after ​hitting naval mines on the “unauthorised route” in the strait. “Even in the event a deal is struck, an increase ‌in ⁠flows through the waterway would still depend on mine clearance, insurance costs and whether or not shipowners would even be willing to take the risk,” LSEG analysts said in a November 10 note. “Meanwhile, attacks have not slowed.” In the previous session, oil prices initially fell by more than $3 a barrel after US officials downplayed the need for further military strikes against Iran, but then regained some of those losses after an Iranian security official said no talks were taking place between the two sides. US crude oil stocks rose in the latest week, market ​sources said, ⁠citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Crude stocks rose by 9 million barrels in the week ended November 6, the sources said. In Russia, oil refining capacity has been reduced by about 30% since ⁠late ​October following renewed Ukrainian drone attacks, industry sources said. Russian and Ukrainian officials met in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for their first peace talks since February, as US President Donald Trump’s envoys launched a fresh push to end the war.

items.title: Oppon Memorial Senior High School celebrates 50 years of educational excellence, resilience
items.description: Nestled within the historic and revered enclave of Kokofu in the Bekwai Municipality in the Ashanti region, Oppon Memorial Senior High School (OMESS) has triumphantly commemorated its milestone 50th Golden Jubilee Anniversary. Held under the inspiring and resonant theme, “Changing the Narrative: 50 Years of Nurturing Greatness for a Brighter Future,” the grand anniversary durbar was an impressive convergence of tradition, academia, and leadership. The ceremonial grounds buzzed with energy as past and present students, dedicated faculty, traditional leaders, clergy, alumni (OMESS Old Students Association), and key officials from the Ghana Education Service (GES) gathered to pay homage to the institution’s rich history. Delivering a heartfelt address, the Headmaster, Richard Ahenkorah, paid glowing tribute to the trailblazing founding fathers, former heads, pioneer staff, and resilient alumni whose monumental sacrifices laid the school’s bedrock. However, balancing celebration with realistic candor, Mr. Ahenkorah highlighted critical infrastructural deficits currently crippling the institution, earnestly appealing for urgent government and private intervention to safeguard an effective teaching and learning environment. Professional Ethics The event served as a solemn platform for national and local leaders to address systemic challenges within the educational sector: The Bekwai Municipal Director of Education, Leticia Obeng, delivered a firm, cautionary address highlighting the Ghana Education Service (GES) code of conduct. She sternly admonished teachers against compromising ethical boundaries, emphasising that professional discipline and student safeguarding must remain paramount. Legislative Support The Member of Parliament for the Bekwai Constituency, Ralph Opoku-Adusei, reaffirmed his unwavering commitment to youth empowerment through strategic investments in educational infrastructure across the constituency. Civic Responsibility The Bekwai Municipal Chief Executive (MCE), Salia Salifu, urged the youth to passionately prioritize their studies while steadfastly abstaining from substance abuse and destructive social vices. Alumni Impact Demonstrating enduring devotion to their alma mater, the OMESS Old Students Association proudly commissioned and handed over a newly constructed, fully furnished two-bedroom quarters for the Assistant Headmaster. Unveiling the facility, a Senior Old Boy, Akwasi Amofa Agyemang, affirmed that “the old students have consistently spearheaded interventions to bolster developmental initiatives here, and we remain unflinchingly dedicated to driving the school’s structural development for generations to come.” The Golden Jubilee climaxed with a vibrant awards ceremony, where distinguished current and former teaching staff, dedicated non-teaching personnel, illustrious alumni, and high-achieving students were conferred with prestigious honors for their selfless service and exceptional academic performance.
