items.title: Economic stability will take time to reflect in Ghanaians’ lives – Bokpin
items.description: Economics professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin says Ghanaians will have to wait to feel the benefits of economic stability because the recovery has relied heavily on government spending cuts. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he said the government had made progress. But the approach had squeezed demand while leaving infrastructure constraints unresolved. “It’s simply because the approach we have adopted in restoring macroeconomic stability is going to take a while to reflect in the lives of Ghanaians.” His assessment comes ahead of the 2027 Budget, scheduled for presentation on Thursday, November 12. Government says it will introduce a four-year New Economy programme centred on investment in productive sectors. The Minority in Parliament has questioned how the proposed US$10 billion programme will be financed. Led by Dr Mohammed Amin Adam, it has demanded a detailed funding plan. It also cited shortfalls in capital spending and questioned funding secured for the existing 24-Hour Economy initiative. Prof Bokpin said lower inflation alone could not capture the difficulties people face daily. “If somebody is spending nine to 12 hours to travel from here to Kumasi, inflation of 5.2% means nothing to that person.” He explained that spending cuts could bring inflation down by reducing demand. But that approach did not expand the economy’s constrained capacity to produce. “If you choose that approach, you will get the result, but the impact will not be felt by Ghanaians.” For a country with a huge infrastructure deficit, he argued, prolonged spending restraint carried a cost. Government investment remained necessary to address constraints holding back growth. “So, for a country that is saddled with a huge infrastructure deficit, imposing restrictions on the growth drivers of the economy, such a country cannot celebrate extensive austerity expenditure cuts.” Despite those concerns, Prof Bokpin credited the government with largely delivering on its initial stabilisation objective. He pointed to falling inflation and interest rates. He also said the cedi was holding its own against major trading currencies despite renewed pressure. The government, he noted, had set aside 2025 and 2026 to restore macroeconomic stability. Spending cuts featured heavily in both years. “To that extent, and to the extent that that is what we are set out to achieve in the first two years of the administration, I would say they’ve done quite well in restoring macroeconomic stability.” He said that progress explained the government’s proposed move towards economic transformation through the New Economy agenda.

items.title: Hidden cause of economic imbalances
items.description: GROWING inequality is a serious economic and social issue. Internally, we tend to treat poverty and inequality as separate problems. They are closely connected but not identical. Poverty is about deprivation; inequality is about how income, wealth, opportunities, and economic power are dis­­tributed. An economy can grow and even red­u­­ce poverty temporarily while allowing wealth and privilege to become concentrated. Household data underlines the problem. The consumption-based Gini coefficient increased from 28.4 in 2018 –19 to 32.7 in 2024 –25. This figure does not capture the full extent of inequality in income and wealth, be­­cause household surveys tend to underrepresent the assets and incomes of the richest households. The distribution of income and wealth influences what people consume, what businesses produce, where investment flows, and how much a country imports. In Pakistan, a relatively small segment commands a disproportionately large share of purchasing power and assets, while much of the population struggles to meet basic needs. A relatively small segment commands a disproportionately large share of purchasing power and assets. The benefits of economic growth have been distributed unevenly. Expanding sectors such as banking, telecommunications, IT, energy, oil and gas require capital, technology, and specialised skills, favouring those who already possess financial resources or access to quality education. The state’s failure to provide decent education and healthcare has denied much of the population a fair opportunity to participate in these activities. Hence, economic disadvantages are passed from one generation to the next. Equally damaging is the continued protection of selected businesses from competition through high import duties, subsidies, tax exemptions, and special regulatory concessions. Powerful business groups have resisted competition, sometimes forming cartels to influence prices and markets. Profits earned through state protection rather than efficiency reward influence instead of innovation, raise costs for consumers, and weaken competitiveness. The tax system has reinforced these inequalities by treating similar incomes from different sources unequally. Salaried individuals face substantial income taxes, while earnings from property, capital gains, and certain commercial activities have historically enjoyed relatively favourable treatment. The state itself has been a major contributor to wealth concentration. Valuable public land and plots have been given to officials and influential individuals, while discretionary powers over building permissions, zoning regulations, and public contracts have created opportunities for private enrichment. Rising property prices, reinforced by speculative investment and the use of real estate to park undeclared wealth, have further increased the fortunes of existing asset owners. Corruption, smuggling, tax evasion, and manipulation of import and export prices have provided additional avenues for accumulating wealth, often beyond the reach of effective taxation and accountability. Together, these factors constitute a system in which public authority is used to transfer economic opportunities and resources to privileged groups. The consequences extend beyond unfair income distribution; they also distort how the economy allocates and uses its scarce resources. When fortunes can be made through political connections, regulatory concessions, and protection from competition, capital and entrepreneurial talent are diverted towards securing favours rather than productive investment. It becomes more profitable to lobby for higher import duties or special exemptions than to invest in technology, improve quality, or develop export markets. The concentration of purchasing power also shapes the structure of domestic demand and, therefore, what businesses choose to produce. Businesses often respond to this purchasing power by directing investment towards activities serving a narrow market. Meanwhile, the limited purchasing power of the majority constrains demand for mass-consumption goods, discouraging investment in industries that could serve a broader domestic market, create jobs, and compete globally. This distorted pattern of consumption and production also contributes to our recurring external imbalances. The concentration of disposable income generates demand for imported vehicles, electronics, luxury goods, foreign travel, and education abroad, adding to the foreign exchange needed for machinery, fuel, technology, and industrial inputs. Not all imports are undesirable. Many are essential for productivity and exports. However, our consumption and production structures generate substantial demand for foreign exchange without a corresponding capacity to earn it through competitive exports. Remittances from overseas Pakistanis have helped bridge this gap. But however valuable these inflows, they cannot substitute indefinitely for an economy capable of financing its import requirements through its own export earnings. Inequality is certainly not the sole cause of external deficits. Exchange rate policies, tariffs, energy costs, inflation, low productivity, and weak export competitiveness also matter. Still, the concentration of purchasing power helps explain why import demand remains substantial even when we face severe foreign exchange constraints. There is another damaging effect. When influential groups secure tax exemptions, subsidies, and protected markets, government revenues suffer. The burden of financing an oversized, extractive state, with its extensive controls and perks and privileges, consequently falls disproportionately on salaried workers, compliant businesses, and ordinary consumers unable to escape taxation. Public expenditure compounds the problem. Chronic underinvestment in quality education and healthcare has denied millions of children a fair start. Affluent households can purchase good private education and medical care, while poorer families depend on poor and overstretched public services. Their children’s prospects depend on family circumstances. The failure to provide equal opportunities thereby perpetuates inequality across generations. Addressing these disparities does not mean pe­­nalising wealth creation. It means distinguishing wealth earned through enterprise, innovation, and productivity from fortunes accumulated through political connections, monopolies, and state-gra­nted privileges. This requires a fairer tax system. Protection must give way to competition, while discretionary allocations of public land, contracts, and regulatory concessions need to be replaced by transparent, rule-based processes. Foreign aid, remittances, and favourable global developments have provided only temporary relief, enabling successive governments to shelve tough reforms, thereby sustaining an economic structure that rewards privilege over productivity. Unless this system of privileges and unequal opportunities is dismantled, Pakistan will remain trapped in recurring internal and external imbalances, regardless of how many stabilisation programmes it negotiates with the IMF and others. The writer is a former governor of the State Bank. Published in Dawn, November 11th, 2026

items.title: What money bought
items.description: SLEAZE, bribery, and secret alliances allegedly marked Trump’s Middle East policy in his first term, and set him on the road to an illegal and unwinnable war against Iran in his second. The central characters in that sordid set of machinations were his own son-in-law and senior adviser Jared Kushner, a few Gulf rulers, and Israel’s prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu — all working towards a plan to redraw the political map of West Asia. Iran was the adversary to be contained, and it was on this that they converged: a plan to “blow up Obama’s Iran nuclear deal”. Billions of dollars were allegedly paid to Kushner in what may be the biggest scandal in recent history — one that best defines the link between money and Trump’s conduct of his Middle East policy, and which has pushed the entire region into an intractable conflict with global consequences. A recently published book, Princes and Thieves by investigative journalist Matthew Cole, provides startling details on how billions of dollars were allegedly transferred into accounts — managed by Kushner — by Gulf sheikhdoms, to implement a plan to break Obama’s nuclear deal with Iran and change the “political map of the Middle East”. The author supports his view of the transactions with details drawn from accounts hacked by a Western intelligence agency, though Kushner has called the allegations fabricated. According to the author, the transfers began in 2017 and were well underway by the spring of 2018, during Trump’s first term — when Kushner served as the president’s special envoy on the Middle East. While he had very close relations with Israel, he also cultivated strong business and diplomatic connections with willing Gulf sheikhdoms to allegedly pay for influence with the Trump administration. >A recent book details how money and corruption were leveraged to redesign the Middle East. According to the author, “Kushner, UAE ruler Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ), and Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) of Saudi Arabia, converged at an auspicious moment. MBS wanted to be crown prince. MBZ wanted to blow up Obama’s Iran nuclear deal, and Kushner wanted both to help him force the Palestinians into a deal that Israel would accept”. The convergence against Obama’s nuclear deal with Iran — formally the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) — brought Saudi Arabia and the UAE together on the issue. Agreed on July 14, 2015, between Iran and the P5+1, and endorsed by Security Council Resolution 2231, the deal came into effect in January 2016. Under it, Iran capped its enrichment at 3.67 per cent, cut its centrifuge numbers and opened its nuclear facilities to IAEA inspection. In return, nuclear-related sanctions on Iran were lifted on oil exports, banking, and SWIFT access, with frozen assets to be released in stages. But Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE had strong reservations. Each opposed the JCPOA for different reasons and with different intensity; the common ground was that the agreement was too narrow and too temporary, its restrictions written to expire under sunset clauses. Israel openly campaigned against it, and the two Gulf states lobbied against it too. For deal sceptics, Trump’s election in 2016 was good news. In May 2018, the president withdrew from the JCPOA and reimposed sanctions in phases under a “maximum pressure” campaign. The move brought the Gulf nations closer to the Trump administration. The billions alleged to have flowed into Kushner’s accounts appeared to have delivered. The book maintains that early in Trump’s first term, “MBZ and MBS offered to pay for a slush fund dedicated to helping the new administration with foreign policy goals”. Both Arab rulers saw this as part of an effort to help Trump win a second presidency. In the same period, Kushner conceived the so-called Abraham Accords aimed at normalisation between Israel and the Arab states. He owned the file. No State Department desk, no regional bureau, no ambassador in the chain: a son-in-law with a security clearance and a direct line to the president negotiated directly with the Gulf rulers, according to the book. One goal was to sideline the question of a separate Palestinian state. The UAE, Bahrain, Morocco, and Sudan signed. The book also reveals that during that period Kushner helped negotiate a secret warming of diplomatic relations between Israel and the UAE — the arrangement that later became public as the Abraham Accords. Cole writes that “Kushner helped negotiate an agreement by Israel to help defend the UAE against a major Iranian military attack. The UAE needed to cover the cost of that emergency defence, and its government secretly made another transfer to Israel’s Central Bank. This was something like a rainy-day defence fund. Combined, the three accounts represented a secret foreign policy negotiated by Kushner with the leaders of Israel, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia. “Although Kushner’s position as senior adviser to the president was unpaid, he was an official government employee. Not only did his position require financial disclosure for ethics regulations, but each year he worked in the White House he had to file both a public and a confidential financial form, the Executive Branch Personnel Public Financial Disclosure Report, known as a 278e disclosure. Because he had access to classified government secrets, Kushner was required to disclose any bank account to which he had signatory — or beneficiary — access.” But apparently, the president’s son-in-law did not comply. The writer quotes a source that Kushner “promised MBZ he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalisation with Israel so that business could take off”. For the Gulf Arab governments, money was not a problem. “The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent,” the source told the author. The book exposes the sordid linkage between power and corruption that marked Trump’s presidency. It also lays bare the unholy alliance between Israel and the Gulf governments, formed to change the political map of the Middle East. In the end, this design has left the region more destabilised than before. The writer is an author and journalist. zhussain100@yahoo.com X: @hidhussain Published in Dawn, November 11th, 2026

items.title: 64% of Ghanaians oppose creation of new districts – CLGA survey
items.description: A survey by the Centre for Local Governance Advocacy (CLGA) has found that 64 per cent of respondents believe Ghana’s 261 Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs) are sufficient and do not support the creation of additional districts. The findings point to limited public appetite for expanding the country’s local government structure, with attention instead turning to whether existing assemblies have the resources and institutional capacity to deliver on their development responsibilities. The survey also raises concerns about political influence in the decentralisation process, with 81 per cent of respondents identifying political interference as a significant factor in the creation of new districts. Chief Executive Officer of the Institute of Chartered Accountants, Ghana, Dr Eric Oduro Osae, has questioned the rationale for establishing more districts, arguing that increasing the number of administrative units does not automatically translate into stronger local economies or improved development outcomes. He said the capacity of existing assemblies to fulfil their responsibilities should be assessed before any decision is taken to expand the country’s administrative structure. “The creation of a new district does not automatically create a stronger local economy, a functioning health facility, a reliable water supply, improved roads, better schools or employment opportunities,” he said. The Head of Research at CLGA, Isaac Owusu, who led the survey, said the findings reflected growing concerns among citizens about the direction of Ghana’s decentralisation process and the priorities informing the creation of new districts. He said about 64 per cent of respondents opposed the creation of additional districts, while 87 per cent called for a freeze on the establishment of new ones. Mr Owusu also drew attention to the finding that 81 per cent of respondents believed political interference influenced decisions to create new districts. He said the findings raised questions about whether the process was being guided primarily by the development needs of communities or by political considerations. The survey adds to the debate about the effectiveness of Ghana’s decentralisation system and whether creating more administrative units necessarily leads to better local governance, improved public services and development at the community level.

items.title: Ghana cannot celebrate austerity amid huge infrastructure deficit – Bokpin
items.description: Economics Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin says Ghana cannot celebrate spending cuts while a huge infrastructure deficit continues to hold back growth and burden citizens. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he acknowledged the government’s progress in stabilising the economy. But he warned that its heavy reliance on expenditure cuts would delay the benefits for ordinary Ghanaians. “For a country that is saddled with a huge infrastructure deficit, imposing restrictions on the growth drivers of the economy, such a country cannot celebrate extensive austerity expenditure cuts.” His comments come ahead of Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson’s presentation of the 2027 Budget on Thursday, November 12. The government plans to unveil a four-year New Economy programme, with investments in productive sectors intended to move Ghana from stabilisation to transformation. The Minority in Parliament has questioned how the programme will be financed. It wants the government to account for existing flagship initiatives, including the 24-Hour Economy, before making fresh commitments. It has also challenged the connection between improving economic indicators and household living conditions. Prof Bokpin said the 2026 Budget, like its predecessor, relied heavily on spending restraint to restore stability. He explained that this approach reduced demand without addressing the economy’s limited production capacity. “You cool the economy. You are shrinking aggregate demand as a way of also bringing inflation down, rather than expanding the economy’s severe or restricted supply capacity.” He argued the consequences were evident in the gap between lower inflation and commuters’ daily frustrations. “If somebody is spending nine to 12 hours to travel from here to Kumasi, inflation of 5.2% means nothing to that person.” For people enduring difficult journeys, better economic figures would offer little immediate comfort. “It’s simply because the approach we have adopted in restoring macroeconomic stability is going to take a while to reflect in the lives of Ghanaians.” Still, Prof Bokpin credited the government with delivering much of its initial stabilisation agenda. He cited falling inflation and interest rates, alongside a cedi that remained relatively resilient despite pressure. He said the administration had set 2025 and 2026 as the years to restore stability. Its approach was also consistent with the IMF-supported programme. “To that extent, and to the extent that that is what we are set out to achieve in the first two years of the administration, I would say they’ve done quite well in restoring macroeconomic stability,” he said.

items.title: Fazlur Rehman’s son skips NAB summons
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Defying a summons from the Na­­tional Accountability Bu­­reau (NAB), Asad Meh­m­ood, son of Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam (JUI-F) chief Mau­lana Fazlur Rahman, fai­­led to appear before the anti-graft watchdog on Monday in a case concerning alle­ged irregularities in appoi­ntments at Pakistan Post. NAB, meanwhile, remained tight-lipped about its next course of action. In such cases, the bureau usually issues second and third notices before taking punitive action, including arrest, if the accused continues to ignore the summons. Mr Mehmood had been directed to appear before the investigation team at 11am on Nov 10 to explain his position on alleged irregularities in 4,252 appointments made at Pakistan Post during his tenure as federal minister in 2022-23. When contacted, a senior NAB official declined to disclose the bureau’s future course of action, saying that under the new laws, details of investigations could not be shared with the media until the relevant court had decided the case. According to the notice, the Establishment Division had authorised recruitment against 3,938 posts at Pakistan Post, but 4,252 people were allegedly appointed, exceeding the approved strength. Of these, 2,646 appointments were reportedly made against posts that had already been abolished, in violation of a cabinet committee’s directions. The bureau is also examining allegations that permanent appointments were made despite a recommendation for contractual recruitment, placing an additional financial burden on Pakistan Post. The alleged political affiliations of some selected candidates are also under scrutiny. items.title: Opposition moves
items.description: THE opposition alliance TTAP has hinted at another anti-government drive . Its recent talks with the JUI-F on parliamentary coordination indicate that the party’s chief Maulana Fazlur Rahman is poised to lead the campaign. All this raises obvious questions: is the opposition seriously planning an anti-government drive? Is it actually convinced that such a movement at this time can remove the government? Will the pragmatic JUI-F chief join such an effort? At least for now, the answer may disappoint the opposition’s supporters. The PTI is locked in a protracted battle with the government, while much of its top leadership remains behind bars. It has twice attempted to mobilise public support for a mass movement and rally people around its political objectives since the controversial February 2024 elections, but both attempts failed. It is obvious that people, particularly in Punjab and Sindh, are not ready to join any such movement at this time. Even in KP, where the PTI had been in power since 2013, the party has failed to mobilise the public. The Jamaat-i-Islami’s drive against high petrol prices similarly failed to bring people out onto the streets. Though the JUI-F has staunch supporters on the streets who are ready to answer their party’s call, its leader has never been one to take needless risks. His azadi march against the PTI government brought thousands of supporters to Islamabad, but failed to dislodge the Imran Khan administration. The sit-in was eventually called off without achieving its objective. The federal government has imposed emergency measures and governor’s rule in KP, claiming they were necessary for security and administrative reasons. The opposition sees these moves as an assault on provincial autonomy. Maulana Fazlur Rahman is actively opposing the move. The government’s response to his criticism has fuelled fears that the JUI-F could face the same crackdown as the PTI. Those concerns are not difficult to understand. The recent actions of the Balochistan government against JUI-F Senator Kamran Murtaza on a questionable citizenship claim reinforce these fears. Yet expectations of the maulana leading another street confrontation with the government anytime soon are likely to remain wishful thinking. Nevertheless, this consensus of politicians of different persuasions reflects a growing frustration with the government’s high-handed actions. The lawyers’ emergence in this arena is particularly significant. The All Pakistan Lawyers Action Committee in Quetta has vowed to support Senator Murtaza and resist any attempt to undermine constitutional supremacy. There are also reports of raids on lawyers’ homes. Although the prospects of a new anti-government movement remain remote, public discontent should not be ignored. Small, isolated protests and expressions of dissent can gradually gather momentum and develop into a much larger movement. Published in Dawn, November 11th, 2026

items.title: We need government to spend to stimulate growth – Bokpin
items.description: Economics Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin has urged the government to spend to stimulate growth, warning that cuts to expenditure are delaying the benefits of economic stability for Ghanaians. Speaking on JoyNews’ PM Express on Tuesday, he acknowledged improvements in key economic indicators. But he said Ghana’s infrastructure deficit required investment to remove barriers to growth. “We need government to spend to stimulate growth,” he said. His call comes ahead of Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson’s presentation of the 2027 Budget on Thursday, November 12. The government plans to unveil a four-year New Economy programme focused on investment in productive sectors. The Minority in Parliament has questioned how the programme will be financed. It wants the government to account for existing flagship initiatives, including the 24-Hour Economy, before introducing fresh commitments. Prof Bokpin said the government’s stabilisation approach had relied heavily on spending cuts in both 2025 and 2026. He argued that approach carried consequences for households and businesses. “So, for a country that is saddled with a huge infrastructure deficit, imposing restrictions on the growth drivers of the economy, such a country cannot celebrate extensive austerity expenditure cuts.” He explained that cutting expenditure could lower inflation by weakening demand. However, it would not necessarily expand the economy’s limited capacity to produce. “You are shrinking aggregate demand as a way of also bringing inflation down, rather than expanding the economy’s severe or restricted supply capacity.” For him, that distinction explains why improved economic figures may offer little comfort to people facing poor roads and lengthy journeys. “If somebody is spending nine to 12 hours to travel from here to Kumasi, inflation of 5.2% means nothing to that person.” He said the benefits of the current approach would take time to reach Ghanaians. “It’s simply because the approach we have adopted in restoring macroeconomic stability is going to take a while to reflect in the lives of Ghanaians.” Despite those concerns, Prof Bokpin credited the government with making progress towards its stated two-year stabilisation objective. He cited falling inflation and interest rates, alongside a currency that remained relatively resilient despite renewed pressure. “I would say they’ve done quite well in restoring macroeconomic stability,” he added. He said the government’s proposed New Economy reflected its intention to move from stabilisation towards economic transformation.

items.title: Agadir: Plus de 6,73 millions de nuitées touristiques dans les EHTC à fin septembre
items.description: Les établissements d’hébergement touristique classés (EHTC) de la ville d'Agadir ont enregistré 6.730.490 nuitées touristiques lors des neuf premiers mois de 2026, en hausse de 9% par rapport à la même période de l'an dernier, a indiqué l’Observatoire national du tourisme. Ce volume représente 19% de l’ensemble des nuitées touristiques enregistrées dans les établissements hôteliers classés à l’échelle nationale, plaçant Agadir à la deuxième position, derrière Marrakech (32%), a précisé l'observatoire. Pour le mois de septembre dernier, les EHTC d'Agadir ont enregistré 751.682 nuitées touristiques, en hausse de 8% par rapport à septembre 2025, a souligné la même source, notant que le taux d'occupation de ces établissements a atteint 76%. Au niveau de la région Souss-Massa, le nombre total de nuitées touristiques s’est établi, lors des neuf premiers mois de 2026, à 7,21 millions, en hausse de 9% en glissement annuel, représentant une part de 21% à l’échelle nationale, tandis que le taux d’occupation s’est établi à 70%. Au niveau national, le nombre de nuitées touristiques enregistrées par les EHTC a atteint 34,83 millions à fin septembre dernier, en hausse de 7% par rapport aux neuf premiers mois de 2025, avec un taux d’occupation de 58%. items.title: Former Magistrate Mary Bibiana Oduro to be buried November 20
items.description: The late Her Worship Mary Bibiana Ama Ansomaa Oduro, a former Magistrate of the Judicial Service of Ghana and accomplished entrepreneur, will be buried on Friday, November 20, 2026. She was 75. According to funeral arrangements released by the family, a filing past will take place at 8 a.m., followed by a burial service at 9 a.m. at Agape House New Testament Church, Pawpaw Street, East Legon, Accra. She will be laid in state at her residence at No. 9 Ashiokor Link, North Dzorwulu, from 4 a.m. to 7 a.m. The final funeral rites will be held at the Underbridge immediately after the burial service. A thanksgiving service will take place at 11 a.m. on Sunday, November 22, at the same church, after which the final funeral rites will continue at her residence. The dress code for Friday’s funeral is black, while mourners attending Sunday’s thanksgiving service are expected to wear black and white. Born on January 6, 1951, to the late Yaw Oduro of Kwahu Twenedurase and the late Matilda Lamley Mensah of Ngleshi Adanse, Jamestown, Accra, Mary Oduro built a distinguished career spanning public administration, banking, commerce, entrepreneurship and the Judiciary. She received her early education at Bishop’s Girls’ School in Accra before proceeding to St Mary’s Girls’ Secondary School at Korle-Gonnor. Her professional career began as Secretary to the Minister of Trade before she joined Standard Bank, now Standard Chartered Bank. In 1974, she moved to Willowbrook Ghana Limited, a British bus assembly company based at Dzorwulu, as its first secretary. She later rose through the ranks to become the company’s Commercial Manager. Outside her corporate career, she established Shaker Spot, a fashion design business that gained popularity for its distinctive creations throughout the 1990s. She also made significant contributions to international trade between Ghana and Nigeria, supplying consumer goods and fashion products to major retailers, including GNTC and CFAO Multistores. One of the defining chapters of her life was her decision to pursue a career in law later in life. In the early 2000s, she obtained a first degree, majoring in Political Science and Sociology, before proceeding to the Makola School of Law. She subsequently joined the Judicial Service of Ghana as a Magistrate. She served at the District Magistrate Courts in Osu and Saltpond for almost a decade before moving to Accra, where she worked within the Family and Juvenile Court system. Beyond her professional accomplishments, Mary Oduro was remembered as a gentle, compassionate and generous woman who placed great value on family, friendship and service to others. She is survived by three children: Nii Amaah Addo (Mergash), Amanda Nana Akyere Addison and Nana Akosua Asantewaa Assiamah Owusu (MizSanty). Her late daughter, Barbara Nana Adwoba Addison, is also named in the family notice. The family has invited former colleagues, friends, sympathisers and members of the public to join them in celebrating her life and paying their final respects. Her Worship Mary Bibiana Ama Ansomaa Oduro passed away on September 9, 2026.

items.title: ‘Government has done quite well’ in restoring macroeconomic stability – Bokpin
items.description: Economics Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin says the government has done well to restore macroeconomic stability, citing falling inflation, lower interest rates, and the cedi’s relative resilience. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he said the gains reflected the administration’s stated priority for its first two years. “I would say they’ve done quite well in restoring macroeconomic stability.” Assessing performance against the 2026 Budget, Prof Bokpin said there was clear evidence of progress. Inflation and interest rates had fallen. The cedi was also holding its own against major trading currencies despite renewed pressure. But he cautioned that stabilisation remained a work in progress. “The question is, we are still restoring macroeconomic stability. Let me put it that way,” he said. His assessment comes ahead of the 2027 Budget, which Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson is scheduled to present on Thursday, November 12. The budget is expected to outline the government’s New Economy agenda and priorities for jobs and investment. The Minority has questioned how the government plans to finance the agenda and demanded an account of existing flagship programmes. It argues that improvements in economic indicators have yet to translate into better living conditions. Prof Bokpin also highlighted the limits of the government’s approach. He said the 2025 and 2026 budgets relied heavily on spending cuts to restore stability. He explained that this approach reduced demand and helped bring inflation down. But it also constrained spending needed to address infrastructure gaps and stimulate growth. “If you choose that approach, you will get the result, but the impact will not be felt by Ghanaians.” He pointed to difficult journeys on major roads as an example of why better economic figures may offer little comfort. “If somebody is spending nine to 12 hours to travel from here to Kumasi, inflation of 5.2% means nothing to that person.” He said the method used to stabilise the economy meant households would have to wait for the benefits. “It’s simply because the approach we have adopted in restoring macroeconomic stability is going to take a while to reflect in the lives of Ghanaians.” Still, Prof Bokpin said the government had largely delivered on its initial stabilisation objective. He described that objective as consistent with the IMF programme. He linked the proposed New Economy agenda to the government’s intention to move from stabilisation into economic transformation.

items.title: Rain, snow in northern parts of the country from today
items.description: RAWALPINDI: The Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) has forecast rain, wind and thunderstorms, with snowfall over the hills, in the upper parts of the country over the next two to three days, urging the authorities concerned to take precautionary measures to prevent any untoward incident, particularly in hilly areas. According to the Met Off­ice, a shallow westerly wave is approaching the western and northern par­ts of the country. The system is likely to intensify on Nov 12 and may persist over the upper regions until the morning of Nov 14. In Khyber Pakhtu­nk­hwa, under the influence of this weather system, rain, wind and thundersto­rms, accompanied by isolated heavy falls and hailstorms, are expected in Dir, Chitral, Swat, Koh­is­t­an, Shangla, Battagram, Mansehra, Abbottabad, Haripur, Buner, Malak­and, Bajaur, Mohmand, Kohat, Peshawar, Charsa­dda, Nowshera, Mar­dan, Swabi, Khyber, Orakzai, Kurram, Hangu, Lakki Mar­wat, Karak, Bannu, Dera Ismail Khan and Waziristan from the evening/night of Nov 10 until the morning of Nov 14, with occasional breaks. Snowfall is also likely over the mountains during this period. In Punjab and Islamabad, light rain, wind and thunderstorms are expected in the capital city, the Potohar region, Mianwali, Khushab, Bhakkar, Sargodha, Murree and adjoining areas on Wednesday (today). More rain, wind and thunderstorms are forecast for Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Murree, Galiyat, Attock, Chakwal, Jhelum, Mandi Bahauddin, Gujrat, Gujranwala, Hafizabad, Wazirabad, Lahore, Kasur, Sheikhupura, Sialkot, Narowal, Mianwali, Khushab and Sargodha on Nov 12 and 13, with occasional breaks. Rain, wind and thunderstorms are also expected in Dera Ghazi Khan, Layyah, Bhakkar and Multan on Nov 12. Isolated hailstorms are also likely during the period. Snowfall over hills Meanwhile, rain, wind and thunderstorms, accompanied by snowfall over the hills, are expected in Azad Kashmir, including Neelum Valley, Muzaffarabad, Rawalakot, Poonch, Hattian, Bagh, Haveli, Sudhanoti, Kotli, Bhimber and Mirpur, and Gilgit-Baltistan, including Diamir, Astore, Ghizer, Skardu, Hunza, Gilgit, Ghanche and Shigar, until the afternoon of Nov 14, with occasional breaks. Dry weather Mainly dry weather is expected to prevail across most districts of Sindh and Balochistan. However, isolated rain, wind and thunderstorms, accompanied by hailstorms, are expected in Duki, Harnai, Pishin, Sherani, Surab, Zhob, Barkhan, Musakhel, Quetta, Ziarat, Chaman, Qila Abdullah, Qila Saifullah, Kalat and Khuzdar on the night of Nov 11 and Nov 12. Impacts and advisories The Met Office advised farmers to plan their agricultural activities in accordance with the prevailing and forecast weather conditions. It warned that light snowfall over high mountains and glaciers could occur during the wet spell. Foggy conditions are also likely to develop in patches over the plains following the spell. items.title: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Hegseth
items.description: Republicans in the US House of Representatives blocked an effort on Tuesday to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, winning a reprieve for the polarising Pentagon chief before Democrats take control of Congress next year and possibly try again. The vote on a procedural motion came just hours after Hegseth blasted efforts to impeach him as a farce and delivered a defiant defence of his record at the helm of the US military, winning praise from US President Donald Trump. The chamber voted 211 to 204 in favour of a motion to refer eight articles of impeachment to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee, a move that the sponsor of the impeachment push, US Representative Thomas Massie, warned would kill it. Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, had hoped to draw votes from Republicans upset with Hegseth’s policies and wary of the unpopularity of the war on Iran , but no other Republicans joined him. Democrats had voiced strong support for the impeachment effort. But 11 Democrats, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California, did not vote. If eight of them had, the procedural measure would have been defeated, paving the way for a full House impeachment vote. Pelosi’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on why she missed the vote. Trump cheered the results in a social media post, saying the effort to impeach Hegseth “has miserably FAILED!” In a sign that the impeachment episode may have drawn Trump and Hegseth closer together, Trump added that Hegseth’s performance on Iran, Venezuela and other issues “led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot.” Hegseth would have been the first US defence secretary to be impeached. The last time any civilian leader of the US military was impeached was in 1876, when William Belknap held the title “secretary of war”. Hegseth calls himself secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and “woke” when he took office last year. Trump cannot change the name of the Defence Department without approval from Congress. Iran war anger Voter anger over the war on Iran, which has settled into an effective stalemate focused on securing the Strait of Hormuz, helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week’s midterm elections . A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday found a majority of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress, which takes office in January, to act to end the war once and for all. Although Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned the war and blamed it for the Republicans’ midterm rout, he voiced support for Hegseth on Tuesday. “This isn’t about Iran, this is about the fact that Pete took on the bureaucracy at the Pentagon,” Vance wrote on social media. Before the vote, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Monday: “Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America’s national security, and he’s the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran.” Hegseth has repeatedly defended the conflict, calling Trump courageous and saying Iran’s military has been left in ruins. He also said his orders to US forces were lawful, despite Massie’s accusations of “high crimes and misdemeanours” ranging from the war itself to the US military raid in January to depose Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. “History will judge the Iran war quite differently than the conventional wisdom right now,” Hegseth said on Tuesday at his first Pentagon briefing in six months. Jeffries said he would talk to members about whether to mount a new impeachment effort in the next Congress. “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time,” he said. A Democratic-led push to impeach Hegseth could be far more intense, with lawmakers calling in top brass to testify, including generals and admirals fired by Hegseth who have remained silent so far. Hegseth, who has railed against diversity efforts at the Pentagon, fired the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, who is Black, and the Navy’s top admiral, a woman, among others. In such an effort, Democrats could also raise other issues concerning to voters including Pentagon policy toward Ukraine and the US military’s strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats in Caribbean and Pacific waters. Some Republicans say Hegseth’s strained relations with Congress are becoming a political liability as the Trump administration seeks a huge increase in the military’s budget to $1.5 trillion from $950 billion. Massie said he was disappointed by the vote, comparing Republicans to passengers content to go down with the Titanic. “They know it’s a sinking ship but committed to stay on board,” he said.

items.title: Public Accounts Committee seeks to delay power firms’ sell-off until asset valuation
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Pub­lic Accounts Committee (PAC) on Tuesday propo­sed deferring the privatisation of power companies, expected to take place in January, until their assets, machinery, land and other properties are properly assessed and revalued to prevent potential losses to the national exchequer. The proposal came after Auditor General of Paki­stan Maqbool Ahmad Gon­dal raised concerns that the government was relying on outdated valuations of public assets during a meeting of the PAC to examine the audit reports of the Power Division and its attached entities for 2024-25. The committee observed that the management had failed to revalue fixed ass­ets worth Rs624.47 billion. The Auditor General’s office also pointed out that the companies had not tag­ged their assets, reflecting negligence in complying with directives of the Nati­o­nal Electric Power Regul­a­tory Authority (Nepra). It said property, plant and equipment were key components of financial statements, and inaccurate valuations could distort a company’s overall financial position. PAC Chairperson Shah­ida Begum said the actual value of the assets needed to be determined and properly categorised before proceeding with privatisation. “Until we know their exact value, how can we privatise them? If the assets are sold without proper valuation, it will definitely result in a loss for the government,” she said. She called for another meeting in three weeks to review the privatisation process and ensure that the assets were assigned their correct market values before further steps were taken. The Privatisation Commission and the Power Division were directed to submit detailed reports at the next meeting. Rs8.6bn payments questioned The committee also examined audit objections concerning payments of Rs8.648bn borne by electricity consumers because of poor planning, faulty procurement of equipment and deficiencies in the performance of a grid station and its associated transmission line. During a performance audit of the power transmission system for wind projects in the Sindh Wind Corridor, auditors found that Rs8.6bn had been paid to wind power producers under the Non-Pro­ject Missed Volume (NPMV) mechanism. The projects were ready to supply electricity, but the 220kV Jhim­pir Grid Station could not handle their full output because of frequ­ent tripping and system instability. The management attributed the losses to faulty equipment procurement and worsening climate change conditions. MNA Munazza Hassan took exception to the response when National Grid Managing Director Altaf Hussain attributed the loss to climate change. Calling it criminal negligence, MNA Shazia Marri lamented resistance to renewable technologies. Regarding the Rs8.6bn amount, she said the matter had not been settled and that further details would be sought at the next meeting, along with the relevant inquiry report. She said the issue would be taken up again after the required information and assessments had been completed. Published in Dawn, November 11th, 2026

items.title: I was soaked for hours before help came — 74-year-old blind man whose home was wrecked by wind storms
items.description: …Good-spirited man begins rebuilding the house By Chinedu Adonu ENUGU – For 74-year-old Mr. Stephen Ogbo, the rainstorm that ripped through his residence at Ugbo Ezeji, D-Line, Abakpa Nike, Enugu metropolis, was a terrifying, unforgettable experience. The ugly incident left him soaked in water for hours, trapped in a shattered building and unable to find his way to safety because of his blindness. As the storm raged, Ogbo could neither see the destruction around him nor find his way out. He remained helpless until an unidentified female tenant eventually came to his rescue. Recounting his ordeal, Ogbo said the woman approached him after he had spent several hours soaked in water, unable to escape from the disaster. “The female tenant came to me after several hours but couldn’t find any way to escape as a blind man. She said: “Daddy, we have been trapped by the windstorm,” he recalled. According to him, the woman held him, led him out of the destroyed building, and searched for shelter where he could find safety. Although he could not identify his rescuer, he remembered that the voice belonged to a woman. “I do not know the name of the woman who came to my rescue, but the voice was a woman’s voice,” he said. A native of Nomeh Unateze in Nkanu East Local Government Area of Enugu State, Ogbo said he had lived in the compound for about eight years before the incident. The rainstorm damaged the residential building housing 23 families, ripping off its roof and destroying property belonging to tenants. The incident left the occupants struggling to find shelter and salvage their belongings. For the affected families, what began as an ordinary evening quickly turned into a nightmare, with the destruction leaving them with the difficult task of restoring their homes and livelihoods. A cry for help However, days after the incident, help has begun to come following an appeal by the victims for help. Chief Kingsley Chizoba Nweke, the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) senatorial candidate for Enugu East Senatorial District, where the blind man hails from, has commenced the reconstruction of the damaged home after watching a video in which the victims appealed for assistance. Nweke visited the affected residents at Ugbo Ezeji and said their plight moved him to intervene, and announced that building materials had been purchased and contractors mobilised to commence the reconstruction. “It’s a pity, actually. If you look at the roof, it is damaged, and the place is messed up. I saw them interviewed two days ago and they cried out that they needed help. “That touched me so much, so I said it was important that I come to their rescue. We have bought the materials, mobilized the contractors, and the work has already commenced,” he said. He explained that the exercise would involve reinforcing the affected structures and replacing damaged roofs to enable the residents to return to their homes. “My priority is to make sure they get back to their houses and keep living again,” he said. Nweke said the intervention was humanitarian and not politically motivated, insisting that he would have assisted the victims irrespective of their political affiliations. “This is not politically motivated. If they were wearing the caps of a different party and they said they needed help, I would still come. They just need help, not because of party,” he said. He described the intervention as part of his broader humanitarian activities, which he said included supporting people who had lost their jobs and means of livelihood. “I will do more than this. We have been doing more than this already. This is just a minor thing from what we have been doing,” he said. He answered my cry. Another resident and woman leader in the area, Mrs. Promise Ugochukwu, described the incident as devastating. She said the storm occurred between 9pm and 10pm, when strong winds ripped off the roof, and rainwater damaged household belongings. Ugochukwu thanked Nweke for responding to the residents’ appeal, describing his intervention as an answer to their call for help. “When I cried out to my father, Odaa Opuo (Nweke), the man whom I trusted, he answered me,” she said. Ogbo also expressed gratitude to Nweke for the intervention and prayed for God’s guidance in his political career. For the 23 families affected by the disaster, the immediate challenge is to restore their homes, replace damaged belongings, and regain the sense of security they lost when the storm struck. But for Ogbo, the memory of that night will remain tied to the kindness of a woman whose name he may not know, but whose helping hands guided him out of danger. In the aftermath of the destruction, her intervention stands as a reminder that even in moments of helplessness, an unexpected act of kindness can make the difference between despair and hope. The post I was soaked for hours before help came — 74-year-old blind man whose home was wrecked by wind storms appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Asaba massacre and Gen Taiwo’s apology
items.description: The apology by retired Major-General Ahmed Ibrahim Taiwo, son of late Colonel Ibrahim Taiwo, to the people of Asaba over the 1967 massacre by federal troops is a remarkable gesture. At the 59th anniversary on October 7, 2026, Ahmed Taiwo expressed profound regret and apologised on behalf of his father and family for any act of omission or commission that contributed to the tragedy. Major Ibrahim Taiwo was the second-in-command of the Nigerian Army’s 2nd Infantry Division under the overall command of Col. Murtala Mohammed, which pushed Biafran troops out of Asaba. Historical accounts have it that on 7th October 1967, over a thousand unarmed Asaba men and boys, were assembled to chant “One Nigeria” as a declaration of their loyalty to the Federal Military Government. Major Taiwo, with Col. Mohammed’s approval, allegedly gave orders for them to be massacred. Curiously, nine years later on 13th February 1976, Mohammed, then the Military Head of State and Taiwo, his trusted aide and Military Governor of Kwara State, were assassinated in a coup plot led by Col. Buka S. Dimka, their former comrades during the Biafra War. Mohammed and Taiwo reportedly took this dastardly decision in revenge for the role played by an indigene of that area, Major Chukwuma Nzeogwu, the leader of the first military coup in Nigeria, in the murder of the Premier of Northern Nigeria, Sir Ahmadu Bello and other Northern leaders. Military officers from the area had also executed Biafra’s overrunning of the Mid-West and parts of the Western Regions before the tide turned against them. Since the War ended, Asaba people’s pains from this incident have been expressed through various means. One of these was Blood on the Nigeria, a bestseller authored by the late ace journalist, Chief Emma Okocha. The apology, coming from a retired senior military officer, is particularly significant. Rather than defend his father against historical accusations, Gen Taiwo chose acknowledgement, contrition and reconciliation. This is commendable. “I used to come online and start telling people that it happened. I would tell them, ‘My father is the one mentioned. I have all to gain by denying it, but you cannot deny what happened. It is what it is. I have come, in private capacity as Taiwo to render our deepest regrets and apologize on behalf of our father and family for any act of omission or commission on his part that led to this heinous massacre,” Taiwo said. Military necessity cannot justify such atrocities. Col. Taiwo’s son, who served meritoriously in the Nigerian Army, has now demonstrated that military loyalty and filial affection need not obstruct historical truth. Asaba’s paramount ruler, the Asagba, Professor Epiphany Azinge, accepted the apology and publicly forgave the Taiwo family. We urge the community to receive this gesture in good faith. Compassion and forgiveness are virtues, not weaknesses. We urge the Federal Government to issue a formal national apology, establish a memorial and provide appropriate reparative support to affected families and the community. This will help in healing the historical wounds. Nigeria cannot build enduring unity by burying painful history. The post Asaba massacre and Gen Taiwo’s apology appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Avoidable distractions on the political trail, by Rotimi Fasan
items.description: When one observes the actions and utterances of Nigeria’s political actors, their habit of moving in circles, and the people’s preference for sensationalism over substance, it becomes clear why we are not making progress politically. We are back again where we were. We are in the campaign season, and the discourses of our engagement are hardly elevated. We keep repeating the same talking points and recycling the same arguments over and over again and wonder why things remain the same. After almost forty years since he first emerged as a political player on the national space, it is incredible that people and groups opposed to President Bola Tinubu cannot go beyond demanding that he tell them about his familial and academic background. They want to know the school he attended, his schoolmates, and from what loins he was spawned. Important as all of this might be, they cannot be all there is to know about a human being, even if he had simply dropped from the skies. What should children who were abandoned at birth do? Let’s, for the sake of making a point, concede that there have been gaps in the information available in the public space about President Bola Tinubu. Does that necessarily wipe off the other things that have been established about his background? Must everyone be compelled to provide every bit of information about their life where there is enough to show that they did not just materialise from space? What is unheard of about self-fashioning or self-invention? Must every gap or new piece of information about an individual’s life have its origins in criminality? Aren’t there people who, for various reasons, no longer wish to be associated with a part of their past life or identity? Do they have an obligation to explain every bit of that to everyone? There are people today who no longer bear their family names. Others exist who have chosen not to acknowledge their parents. What does that take away from them? It’s their right, whatever their reasons for this. Of what material benefit is knowing who President Bola Tinubu’s father is or the primary or secondary schools he attended to us, now that he has overcome whatever advantages or disadvantages that could have constituted? Even if we’ve not been told that is the case with him, aren’t there people who never knew their parents but have gone on to live very meaningful lives? Bill Clinton never met his father. Barack Obama was raised by his mother and grandmother. He only had to trace his Kenyan ancestry long after his father’s death. The manufactured controversy about his birthplace, religion, or race existed only for a time, and Americans moved beyond it. Friedrich Trump, as well as Donald, his son, who is the current president of America, hid his German ancestry for as long as it served his business interest. That has neither improved nor diminished Trump’s status or performance as president. Bola Tinubu had a very prominent mother—indeed, one more prominent than the mothers of many of those who have been loudest about demanding details of his background. If he chooses to leave things at that, why should that and other questions of origin and educational qualifications be the major points of debate decades after he has become a major political figure? His bachelor’s degree already overrides any primary or post-primary qualifications, which is all the Nigerian Constitution demands of political contestants. Does the repeated demand for these not tell us something about those raising these questions rather than about Bola Tinubu himself? Whatever the gaps might be in President Bola Tinubu’s background, the point is that we know enough about him today to conclude that he is an accomplished Nigerian and a human being. We also know that he is educated enough to be the president of Nigeria, and evidence exists to prove this. Political opponents or even critics who are serious about defeating him and are offering an alternative blueprint of governance must learn to make do with what is available and has been validated by law without taking us back to the dead argument about his academic background. This has been scrutinised, forensically examined, and litigated home and abroad, and neither anything concrete nor useful has come out of it. The debate should move on to serious issues of governance. Alhaji Atiku Abubakar only recently went on the same fishing expedition for the president’s records. That wasn’t the first time. He hired lawyers and lobbyists to the tune of 1.5 million American dollars to demand the release of so-called FBI papers and records on Tinubu, and nothing has come out of these efforts. The courts threw out his case less than a week ago. Now, a political upstart has jumped into the arena with confusing tales about Tinubu’s record. The man, Adetokunbo Pearse, is of the Peoples Democratic Party. To that extent, he can be considered a political ally of Atiku Abubakar. He has in the past been on television and other media platforms to criticise President Tinubu and the All Progressive Congress. He is a Lagosian, and in all the decades since Tinubu’s academic record has been a subject of debate, not for once has he disclosed that he knows anything or has something new to add to the controversy. Then, just days after Atiku’s legal challenge was defeated in the US, he comes up again with the tiring story that Bola Tinubu was never at Chicago State University. How does Adetokunbo Pearse’s claim that he was a lecturer in the programme Tinubu graduated from prove that he has Tinubu’s academic records? His story, like the nature of his association with CSU, is doubtful in every particular. Not even in the face of multiple confirmations from that university that Bola Tinubu was there as a student would a harebrained tale such as Adetokunbo Pearse has to retail sell. His background in English studies could not have qualified him to be a lecturer in Business Administration or Accounting, as he tried to impress. He arrived at CSU at least six years after Tinubu had graduated. If he was there, as he claims, between 1985 and 1990, what did he know of Tinubu’s future activity to have anticipated the controversy that came later with it and sourced ahead for his academic credentials? How did a man who was already a lecturer as far back as 1985 end up a Senior Lecturer at least two decades later in the Department of English at the University of Lagos? What was his rank at CSU? This man’s story is as confusing as he himself looked confused on the programme where he made his astounding claims. He is desperate for attention and should by now be satisfied with his moment in the sun. The post Avoidable distractions on the political trail, by Rotimi Fasan appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: ‘I’ve been wounded, shed tears’ – Lateef Adedimeji speaks on life battles
items.description: Nollywood actor Lateef Adedimeji has disclosed that he is facing a series of challenges. He said this while speaking about personal battles that “no one is aware of.” While appreciating God for the grace to keep going, Lateef explained that his smile doesn’t mean he’s living a perfect life. In an Instagram post on Tuesday night, the actor, who revealed he has been wounded and shed tears, said he won’t let the situation stop him from being happy. “Life hasn’t always been easy, but I won’t let that stop me from being happy. “I’ve been wounded, I’ve shed tears, and I’ve engaged in battles that no one is aware of. But despite everything, I still stand, believe, and smile. “My smile doesn’t mean that life is perfect; rather, it means that I haven’t overcome my obstacles. Give thanks to God for the bravery, grace, and fortitude to keep going.”

items.title: Reductionism and the national question: From grievance to federal reform (II), by Usman Sarki
items.description: “Federalism involves the linking of individuals, groups and polities in lasting but limited union in such a way as to provide for the energetic pursuit of common goals while maintaining the respective integrities of all parties.” — Daniel J. Elazar If restructuring is to serve any useful national purpose, the first task must be to distinguish structural defects from failures of governance. Nigeria is excessively centralised in several respects. The Federal Government carries responsibilities that might more effectively be exercised at lower levels. The fiscal relationship among the tiers requires reconsideration. Security arrangements must reflect the reality that many threats are local. States require greater economic flexibility, while local government autonomy and accountability remain unresolved. The concentration of political competition around control of Abuja also raises the stakes of national elections to unhealthy levels. These are genuine restructuring questions. But restructuring will not automatically eliminate corruption or usher in good governance. It will not by itself produce competent governors, efficient local governments, disciplined civil services, effective policing or accountable legislatures. A badly governed region will remain badly governed merely on a larger geographical scale. This is important because constitutional engineering can become an excuse for avoiding the more uncomfortable question of the integrity of leadership. The so-called national question is therefore about considerably more than tinkering with the map of the country. Nigeria operated a regional system in the First Republic, and that arrangement produced notable achievements. The regions enjoyed substantial autonomy and developed distinctive economic, educational and administrative institutions. But the same period also experienced intense political rivalry, disputed elections and censuses, regional crises and, ultimately, the collapse of the constitutional order. The lesson is not that regionalism failed, nor that it should never be reconsidered. It is that no constitutional arrangement can substitute for political accommodation, institutional integrity and a sound democratic culture. Likewise, later state-creation exercises addressed some minority fears and brought government closer to previously neglected areas. But the multiplication of states also created new minorities, new boundary disputes, fresh grievances, demands for additional states, wastefulness and a high cost of governance. Political structures solve some problems while creating others. That reality should encourage equilibrium and rationality in the restructuring debate. No constitutional design will permanently settle the national question, if indeed it is a “question” capable of final settlement. Countries are continuously negotiated communities. Even old federations periodically reconsider the distribution of authority between their central and sub-national governments. Nigeria should do the same, but through a process anchored in constitutionalism rather than ethnic hegemony, ultimatum and diktat. The more productive approach may therefore be to move away from the language of a single grand restructuring towards a programme of accommodative federal reform. Such reform could include a deliberate review of the legislative lists, greater sub-national responsibility for policing and internal security, more rational fiscal arrangements, incentives for states and local governments to develop their own revenue bases, stronger regional economic cooperation, protection for minorities and a clearer constitutional framework for intergovernmental relations. Some functions could be transferred immediately. Others might be shared. Still others should remain federal because the integrity of the Nigerian state requires common institutions, common standards and a shared national outlook. This would make restructuring an institutional programme rather than an ideological or agitational slogan uttered in abstraction or as an expression of irrational fear and unfounded grievance. There is also a deeper national responsibility. Nigeria cannot be restructured successfully if every community enters the process primarily as a litigant, claimant or aggrieved party and none enters as a stakeholder and custodian of the federation. A durable constitution requires reciprocal sacrifice. The stronger must accept restraints on power. Larger groups must recognise minority fears. Minority communities must also accept that federalism cannot guarantee every community its own exclusive political space. Resource-producing areas deserve fairness, while the federation must preserve mechanisms of national solidarity. Regions or states require autonomy, but the centre must retain sufficient capacity to defend the country, conduct foreign policy, manage macroeconomic stability and protect constitutional rights. The national question is therefore not simply about entitlement; fundamentally, it is also about responsibility. It is not enough to ask, “What are we entitled to?” It is equally necessary to ask, “What are we prepared to concede so that Nigeria may continue to exist as a shared political community?” That second question is rarely asked because proponents of restructuring often approach the subject from maximalist positions and mindsets. There is another danger in reductionism. When every national difficulty is explained through the prism of ethnic marginalisation, Nigerians may eventually lose the ability to recognise problems that are common to them. An unemployed young person in Kano and another in Aba may belong to different ethnic communities, but their economic predicament may arise from the same failures. A farmer threatened by insecurity in Zamfara and another displaced in Benue may experience the crisis through different communal narratives, but both require an effective state to protect them. An entrepreneur in Maiduguri, Enugu or Ibadan confronts many of the same problems of electricity, affordable credit, infrastructure and regulation. The Nigerian condition therefore contains both group grievances and shared national challenges. A mature national conversation must be capable of acknowledging both. Restructuring should not become a mechanism for converting every Nigerian into an ethnic litigant before the federation. Its purpose should be the opposite: to design institutions capable of reducing the importance of ethnic competition in everyday governance. The ultimate test of federal reform is not whether every historical grievance is vindicated or resolved, because that would be impossible. The test is whether Nigerians, wherever they live, can exercise citizenship with dignity; whether communities can govern meaningful aspects of their own affairs; whether minorities are secure; whether resources are distributed fairly; and whether the federation possesses sufficient legitimacy to command voluntary loyalty. That is a more demanding objective than redrawing a map in the name of ethnic chauvinism, regionalism or federal retrenchment. Nigeria certainly needs a new federal conversation. The present system contains contradictions that cannot indefinitely be ignored. But that conversation must resist the temptation to reduce the national question to a competition among grievances or the establishment of priorities among entitlements. History should inform it, but not imprison it, just as identity should be recognised but not weaponised. Consent should legitimise political arrangements, but it must not become a formula for perpetual fragmentation. Restructuring should strengthen the federation rather than merely rearrange the geography of dissent and dissatisfaction. The essential challenge is to convert what has too often been a debate of accusation into a programme of institutional reform. That requires practical questions rather than rhetorical ones. Which powers should remain federal? Which should be devolved? What fiscal responsibilities should accompany devolved authority? How should sub-national policing be supervised? How should minorities be protected within larger regions or states? How should disputes over boundaries and affiliation be settled? What safeguards are required to prevent regional majorities from reproducing, at lower levels, the domination they complain of at the centre? These questions are less dramatic than vacuous declarations about restructuring, but they are far more important. They also reveal why restructuring cannot be treated as a single event. Federal reform is better understood as a process of continuous adjustment. Nigeria may require greater devolution in some areas, stronger national standards in others, and new mechanisms of intergovernmental cooperation where responsibilities overlap. What matters is not ideological purity, but institutional effectiveness. The federation should be judged by whether it enables Nigerians to govern themselves better, not by whether it reproduces a preferred historical arrangement shaped towards a particular ethnic interest. Nigeria’s problems cannot all be blamed on centralisation, nor can all national tensions be resolved by regionalism. Some problems are constitutional. Others are administrative, economic, social or political. Some arise from the conduct of leaders. Others arise from institutional weakness. Still others are brought about by poverty, insecurity, demographic pressure and uneven development. A serious national reform agenda must therefore be broad enough to recognise complexity where it exists. Federalism is not merely about dividing power; it is about creating a durable political community in which diversity can coexist with citizenship. Devolution must be accompanied by responsibility. Fiscal autonomy must be accompanied by accountability. Regional or state authority must be accompanied by minority protection. Local control must be balanced by national standards where fundamental rights and citizenship are concerned. Nor should restructuring become a substitute for democratic legitimacy. Constitutional change must proceed through lawful, broadly accepted and nationally legitimate means. A new federation cannot be created by undermining the democratic foundations upon which the existing one rests. Perhaps the most useful question for Nigerians today is therefore not simply whether the country should be restructured. The question should be: Are we seeking a constitutional settlement that enables different peoples to live together more successfully, or merely constitutional language through which old grievances can be pursued by other means in order to fracture the country? The answer will determine whether restructuring becomes the foundation of Nigeria’s renewal or merely another chapter in the unfinished argument over who owns the country. The post Reductionism and the national question: From grievance to federal reform (II), by Usman Sarki appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Judge allows Trump’s $10bn defamation case against BBC to proceed
items.description: A federal judge in Florida has allowed US President Donald Trump’s defamation case against the BBC to go ahead after the broadcaster sought to dismiss it. But Judge Jeffrey Kuntz dismissed a second claim in the $10bn (£7.5bn) lawsuit under the state’s unfair trade practices law. The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021. Trump called the judge’s ruling a “huge victory” in a Truth Social post on Tuesday. A BBC spokesperson said: “We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage.” The BBC spokesperson added: “We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process.” Judge Kuntz found Trump’s defamation allegations against the BBC sufficient for the case to continue, although he did not make a ruling on the merits of the case. “Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day,” he wrote in Tuesday’s order. Trump’s lawsuit – filed in Florida – accuses the BBC of “intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring” the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021. The BBC apologised and said that the broadcast had given “the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action”. The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US. Along with defamation, Trump claimed in the lawsuit that the broadcaster had violated Florida law, specifically the Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. Kuntz on Tuesday dismissed that part of the lawsuit, ruling that the documentary did not constitute commercial speech.A judge ordered Trump last month to answer questions under oath in the lawsuit by 11 December, after the president cancelled a previous deposition last month, citing “matters of national importance”. A lawyer representing the BBC said in court that Trump was campaigning in Georgia in October on the scheduled day and had “prioritised that” over answering their questions. Earlier this year, Trump’s lawyers conceded they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC’s BritBox subscription service – as they originally argued – or on the BBC’s website, BBC Select or through US broadcasters. Trump ultimately agreed to drop BBC Studios, the broadcaster’s commercial arm, from his defamation lawsuit, after the BBC argued that it had “no role in creating or producing the documentary”.
